about: Narrow nature's facts for the full list, one per species by iNaturalist taxon id. Each is one sentence of 12 to 25 words, written from that species' Wikipedia article and checked against it (November 2026). scripts/build-day-list.mjs copies them into day-list.json and day-list-extra.json. An empty fact says why there isn't one. A wiki link here replaces the one iNaturalist gives.

39.name: Red-crowned Crane
39.fact: China shortlisted it for national animal, but the decision was put off over its scientific name, Grus japonensis, which means Japanese crane.

53.name: Gray Crowned-Crane
53.fact: Along with the black crowned crane, it's the only crane that can roost in trees, thanks to a long hind toe that grips branches.

95.name: White-bellied Korhaan
95.fact: Young birds stay with their parents much longer than those of other bustards in the region, so it's usually seen in pairs or families.

162.name: Sora
162.fact: More often heard than seen, the sora advertises its territory with a loud, squeaky whinny that slows and drops in pitch.

473.name: American Coot
473.fact: Parents favor chicks with the brightest orange-tipped plumes, the first known case of parents selecting for showy ornaments in their young.

871.name: Barbary Partridge
871.fact: It's Gibraltar's national bird and appears on the local penny coins, even though it was introduced there.

906.name: Wild Turkey
906.fact: Pilgrims brought domestic turkeys with them from England, unaware that this larger wild relative was already living in the forests of Massachusetts.

974.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
974.fact: North America's only year-round resident of the alpine zone, it turns completely white in winter.

981.name: Ring-necked Pheasant
981.fact: It's South Dakota's state bird, one of only two US state birds that aren't native to the United States.

1406.name: Gambel's Quail
1406.fact: Often confused with the California quail, the male gives itself away with a black patch on the lower breast that California quail lack.

1409.name: California Quail
1409.fact: Its curving crest is made of six feathers that droop forward, black in males and brown in females.

1428.name: Helmeted Guineafowl
1428.fact: Early European colonists in North America confused the native wild turkey with this African bird.

1626.name: Hoatzin
1626.fact: Chicks escape predators by dropping into the water and swimming away, then climb back to the nest with the two claws on each wing.

1986.name: Greater Roadrunner
1986.fact: Early in the morning it sunbathes, back to the sun and feathers ruffled to bare its black skin, sometimes for two or three hours.

2025.name: Orange-footed Scrubfowl
2025.fact: Only the size of a chicken, it builds nest mounds of sand and leaf litter up to 4.5 meters tall and 9 meters across.

2038.name: Australian Brushturkey
2038.fact: Goannas love its eggs, so they often end up with pecked tails from being chased ferociously off its nest mound.

2068.name: Chestnut-bellied Guan
2068.fact: Found only in Brazil, this guan has a rough, crowlike song and white spots running from its chest to its belly.

2090.name: Plain Chachalaca
2090.fact: Several birds often call a loud, raucous cha-cha-LAW-ka together, which some say sounds like a bunch of men arguing.

2168.name: Turquoise-browed Motmot
2168.fact: Known as the clock bird on the Yucatán Peninsula, it swings its racket-tipped tail like a pendulum to tell predators it's spotted them.

2208.name: Chestnut-headed Bee-eater
2208.fact: Missing the long central tail feathers of most of its relatives, it wears a chestnut crown above a yellow face and throat.

2248.name: White-fronted Bee-eater
2248.fact: Colonies average 200 birds, organized in clans where about half the non-breeders help relatives dig nests, incubate eggs and feed chicks.

2328.name: Gray-headed Kingfisher
2328.fact: It guards its nest hole in a steep riverbank by repeatedly dive-bombing foraging monitor lizards.

2413.name: Laughing Kookaburra
2413.fact: Its laughing territorial call, often given by several birds at once, is widely used as a stock jungle sound effect.

2453.name: Red-backed Kingfisher
2453.fact: A kingfisher that often lives far from water, it digs its nesting burrow into steep banks above dry creek beds.

2464.name: Sacred Kingfisher
2464.fact: The 'sacred' in its name comes from a 1782 claim that Polynesians revered it for haunting their marae and burial grounds.

2753.name: Rose-crowned Fruit Dove
2753.fact: Its pinkish-red crown has a yellow border, set off by a grey head and breast and an orange belly.

2927.name: Oriental Turtle-Dove
2927.fact: The Ainu traditionally hear its call as a saying: 'turtle dove ploughs, grandmother draws water, wife cooks, little master eats'.

3033.name: Stock Dove
3033.fact: A hole-nester in old trees, it's also been found nesting in rabbit burrows, ruins, cliff cracks and nest boxes.

3048.name: Common Wood-Pigeon
3048.fact: In the UK and Ireland its cooing is remembered as 'take two cows, Teddy', though the call starts and ends partway through the phrase.

3460.name: White-winged Dove
3460.fact: North America's only game bird that's also a migratory pollinator, it leans heavily on saguaro nectar and fruit where the cactus grows.

3652.name: Namaqua Dove
3652.fact: A very small dove found over much of sub-Saharan Africa, as well as Arabia and Madagascar.

3740.name: Australian Ibis
3740.fact: Ibises in several regions have learned to eat cane toads by flicking them until they release their toxin, then washing them in water.

3743.name: Hadada Ibis
3743.fact: Named for its extremely loud haa-haa-haa-de-dah call, often given in flight as birds leave and return to roost trees.

3770.name: Green Ibis
3770.fact: It's found today from Costa Rica to northern Argentina, but fossils show it once lived as far north as Kansas.

3786.name: Blue-footed Booby
3786.fact: When researchers dulled a male's blue feet with makeup after the first egg, his mate laid a smaller second one.

3812.name: Magellanic Penguin
3812.fact: Each year the male reclaims last year's burrow and waits for his partner, who can recognize him by his call alone.

3838.name: Little Stint
3838.fact: Its numbers rise and fall with lemmings, because in poor lemming years skuas and snowy owls eat Arctic waders instead.

3849.name: Sanderling
3849.fact: It runs along beaches with a bicycling action of its legs, and unlike other small sandpipers it has no hind toe.

3851.name: Baird's Sandpiper
3851.fact: It migrates 9,300 miles from the Arctic tundra to the southern tip of Argentina and Chile, in as little as five weeks.

3938.name: Ruddy Turnstone
3938.fact: In every season it wears a harlequin pattern of brown, black and white, set on short, bright orange legs.

4180.name: Northern Fulmar
4180.fact: Even as a chick, it can spray foul-smelling stomach oil at predators, matting the feathers of attacking birds and sometimes killing them.

4208.name: Great Crested Grebe
4208.fact: Pairs court each other with elaborate, synchronized dances, showing off striking black, orange-brown and white plumage.

4257.name: American Flamingo
4257.fact: Though it's a Florida icon, it was largely wiped out there by 1900 and is now only an uncommon visitor.

4258.name: Chilean Flamingo
4258.fact: Check the legs: grayish with pink joints, and more than half the bill is black.

4304.name: Pied Cormorant
4304.fact: Its feathers aren't fully waterproof, which may help it stay underwater longer, so it often spreads its wings to dry after diving.

4328.name: Brown Pelican
4328.fact: Theodore Roosevelt set aside Florida's Pelican Island in 1903, the first National Wildlife Refuge, to protect brown pelicans from hunters.

4333.name: Dalmatian Pelican
4333.fact: The 'crispus' in its name is Latin for curly, after the shaggy crest that sets it apart from the smooth-headed great white pelican.

4345.name: Western Gull
4345.fact: It's been seen stealing milk straight from an elephant seal's teat, and it'll snatch fish right out of a pelican's mouth.

4366.name: Slaty-backed Gull
4366.fact: Its wings show a 'string of pearls', large white crescents on the flight feathers that join a broad white trailing edge.

4368.name: Great Black-backed Gull
4368.fact: The largest gull in the world, it's a very aggressive hunter, pirate and scavenger along North Atlantic coasts.

4385.name: California Gull
4385.fact: Utah's state bird, it's remembered for helping Mormon settlers fight a plague of crickets in what's called the Miracle of the Gulls.

4388.name: Kelp Gull
4388.fact: Adults have black upperparts and wings, a yellow bill with a red spot, and greenish-yellow legs that brighten when breeding.

4415.name: Pigeon Guillemot
4415.fact: Its legs, feet and even the inside of its mouth are red, and a dark wedge breaks up its wing patch.

4504.name: Atlantic Puffin
4504.fact: Colonies in Iceland hold 60% of the world's Atlantic puffins, and in their burrows they growl a bit like a chainsaw being revved up.

4569.name: Large-billed Tern
4569.fact: A big, short-tailed tern with a large yellow bill, it lives on rivers and freshwater lakes across most of South America.

4578.name: Northern Jacana
4578.fact: Females are much bigger than males, and each can keep up to four males, who build the floating nests and incubate the eggs.

4604.name: Collared Pratincole
4604.fact: Unusual for a wader, it hunts insects on the wing like a swallow, often near water in the evening.

4627.name: Red-throated Loon
4627.fact: The smallest of the world's loons, it only gets its reddish throat patch in breeding season and is plain grey and white in winter.

4661.name: Dickinson's Kestrel
4661.fact: Also called the white-rumped kestrel, it's mostly dark gray with a pale head and rump, and bare yellow skin around the eye.

4665.name: American Kestrel
4665.fact: Also called the grasshopper hawk for its diet, it sometimes hangs in the air on rapid wingbeats while homing in on prey.

4689.name: Greater Kestrel
4689.fact: Whitish eyes set it apart from any similar bird, and it's drawn to fires to catch insects fleeing the flames.

4711.name: Black-thighed Falconet
4711.fact: About the size of a sparrow, it's one of the smallest birds of prey and usually breeds in an old barbet nest hole.

4754.name: Saddle-billed Stork
4754.fact: Females have golden yellow eyes, while males have brown eyes and dangling yellow wattles, rare color differences for a stork.

4756.name: Turkey Vulture
4756.fact: Flying low, it can sniff out the gases that dead animals give off in the early stages of decay.

4765.name: Black Vulture
4765.fact: Sharp eyes help it find carcasses, and so does tailing other vultures that have a keen sense of smell.

4817.name: Semipalmated Plover
4817.fact: Its partly webbed feet give it its name, and it fakes a broken wing to lure intruders away from its ground nest.

4850.name: Magellanic Oystercatcher
4850.fact: Disturbed near its nest, it may move off and sit on an imaginary one, false-brooding to draw attention away from its eggs and chicks.

4867.name: Southern Lapwing
4867.fact: South America's only crested wader, it has red bony spurs on its wings to intimidate foes and fight birds of prey.

4936.name: White-faced Heron
4936.fact: It reached New Zealand on its own in the late 1940s, and it's the only heron recorded breeding in Tasmania.

4937.name: Little Blue Heron
4937.fact: Despite the 'blue' in its name, young ones stay almost entirely white, like a snowy egret, until their second year.

4943.name: Little Egret
4943.fact: Hunted out of northwestern Europe for hat plumes in the 1800s, it's now breeding again in Britain, Ireland, France and the Netherlands.

4952.name: Cocoi Heron
4952.fact: The largest heron in South America, it's widely called garza mora, or 'black heron', though it's mostly pale grey.

4954.name: Grey Heron
4954.fact: Roast heron was once a prized dish, and 400 were served when George Neville became Archbishop of York in 1465.

4956.name: Great Blue Heron
4956.fact: In South Florida, the Florida Keys and the Caribbean, some are all white, a population known as the great white heron.

4993.name: Indian Pond-Heron
4993.fact: It's been seen picking up bread crumbs and dropping them on the water to bait fish.

4999.name: Yellow-crowned Night Heron
4999.fact: Hunting crayfish, it stands at the burrow facing the sun, so its shadow doesn't fall across the entrance and warn its prey.

5020.name: Green Heron
5020.fact: Listen for a loud, sudden kyow, and look for a chestnut neck often pulled in tight against the body.

5049.name: Bare-throated Tiger-Heron
5049.fact: Its bare throat is greenish-yellow to orange at every age, and males give a booming call, especially at sunset.

5106.name: Eurasian Sparrowhawk
5106.fact: Females are up to 25% larger than males, one of the biggest size gaps between the sexes of any bird.

5167.name: Montagu's Harrier
5167.fact: In flight it usually looks slimmer than a hen harrier, with longer, narrower wings and almost tern-like wingbeats.

5173.name: Western Marsh Harrier
5173.fact: Males often pair with two females and occasionally three, and most pair bonds last just a single breeding season.

5212.name: Red-tailed Hawk
5212.fact: TV shows often use its rasping scream as a generic raptor sound, even when the bird on screen isn't a red-tailed hawk.

5305.name: Bald Eagle
5305.fact: In 2017 a pair in British Columbia adopted a red-tailed hawk chick they'd likely carried home as prey, and it went on to fledge.

5349.name: Snail Kite
5349.fact: When invasive apple snails five times the native size reached the Everglades, the kites there quickly evolved to be 12% bigger.

5366.name: Eurasian Griffon
5366.fact: In soaring flight it burns only about 1.43 times its resting metabolic rate, compared with upwards of 16 times for other birds.

5406.name: Brahminy Kite
5406.fact: To the Iban of Sarawak's Upper Rajang, this kite is the war god Singalang Burung when he comes down to earth.

5479.name: Southern Yellow-billed Hornbill
5479.fact: Walled into her nest with her own droppings, the female sheds every flight feather at once while the male feeds her through a slit.

5914.name: Green-crowned Brilliant
5914.fact: Instead of hovering, it usually clings to a flower to feed, and males sometimes defend patches of Marcgravia vines, a main nectar source.

5947.name: Violet-capped Woodnymph
5947.fact: Males have a glittering violet-blue crown, brilliant green underparts and a steel blue forked tail.

5987.name: Violet Sabrewing
5987.fact: The largest hummingbird in Mexico and Central America, it chases other hummingbirds off sugar-water feeders.

6316.name: Costa's Hummingbird
6316.fact: The male's purple throat feathers flare back behind his head, and he angles his courtship dives to the sun to show them off.

6317.name: Anna's Hummingbird
6317.fact: No other hummingbird has a year-round range this far north, and it rides out snow and subfreezing spells in Seattle.

6369.name: Broad-tailed Hummingbird
6369.fact: Air rushing through two of a male's flight feathers makes a buzzing trill, and in one experiment males without it lost territories more easily.

6915.name: Trumpeter Swan
6915.fact: With fewer than 70 known in the wild in 1933, extinction looked close until aerial surveys found thousands around Alaska's Copper River.

6930.name: Mallard
6930.fact: The wild ancestor of most domestic ducks, and it's been introduced as far away as New Zealand and Australia.

6937.name: Green-winged Teal
6937.fact: One of the smallest dabbling ducks, it gave its name to the blue-green color teal.

6947.name: Yellow-billed Teal
6947.fact: Drakes stretch up high after mating and swim around and alongside the female, a routine unique among its relatives.

6994.name: Barrow's Goldeneye
6994.fact: Males wear a white crescent on a purple-glossed head, while male common goldeneyes show a round white patch and green gloss.

7004.name: Common Merganser
7004.fact: Groups often fish together by forming a semicircle and driving fish into shallow water, where they're easier to catch.

7007.name: Pink-footed Goose
7007.fact: Its most important breeding site, Þjórsárver in Iceland, wasn't found until 1951, when Peter Scott and his team went looking.

7044.name: Ring-necked Duck
7044.fact: Look for the white rings around the male's gray bill, since the cinnamon neck ring is usually hard to see.

7054.name: Lesser Scaup
7054.fact: Its name may come from the hen's discordant 'scaup, scaup' call, or from scalp, a Scottish word for clams and mussels.

7089.name: Canada Goose
7089.fact: A common park bird, it's often called a pest for its droppings, noise, aggression and habit of stalking and begging for food.

7104.name: Hawaiian Goose
7104.fact: Its toes are less webbed than a typical goose's, an adaptation for walking on the cooled lava of its volcanic home.

7117.name: Upland Goose
7117.fact: Darwin noted in On the Origin of Species that the webbing between its toes seemed 'rudimentary in function, though not in structure'.

7176.name: Australian Wood Duck
7176.fact: It nests in tree hollows, and when it's time to leave, the mother flies down and the ducklings leap to the ground after her.

7250.name: Great Blue Turaco
7250.fact: The Mbuti people of the Ituri Rainforest call it kulkoko and believe it warns okapis of danger by calling loudly.

7428.name: Cedar Waxwing
7428.fact: If only one bird at a time can reach a twig's berries, a flock may line up and pass them beak to beak.

7576.name: Bewick's Wren
7576.fact: Once found east to Pennsylvania and Maryland, it's now extremely rare east of the Mississippi River.

7643.name: American Dipper
7643.fact: Able to walk underwater, it's North America's only aquatic songbird, and white-feathered eyelids make its eyes flash when it blinks.

7875.name: Black-hooded Oriole
7875.fact: Spending much of its time up in the tree canopy, it feeds on insects and fruit, especially figs.

8021.name: American Crow
8021.fact: Crows have been seen robbing a river otter, one pecking its tail as a distraction while the others swooped in and stole its fish.

8026.name: Large-billed Crow
8026.fact: In Japan it's considered a pest, ripping open garbage bags and making off with wire coat hangers to build its nests.

8038.name: Pied Crow
8038.fact: The Maasai name for it, ol-korrok, comes from the sound of its harsh karh-karh-karh call.

8088.name: Eurasian Jay
8088.fact: Eurasian jays were the main planters of European oaks before commercial planting, with one bird able to spread over a thousand acorns a year.

8162.name: Northern Fantail
8162.fact: French ornithologist Louis Vieillot named it rufiventris, Modern Latin for 'red-bellied', from a specimen he wrongly believed came from Australia.

8234.name: Steller's Jay
8234.fact: A noted mimic, it often imitates the calls of red-tailed hawks and ospreys, sending other birds fleeing for cover.

8257.name: Grey-headed Bushshrike
8257.fact: Nicknamed the ghostbird, it's a big bushshrike with a massive bill and a mournful hooting call, usually found in denser savannah vegetation.

8335.name: Canada Jay
8335.fact: Each summer it glues thousands of bits of food into bark and lichen with sticky saliva, then finds them by memory, sometimes months later.

8350.name: Yellow-billed Chough
8350.fact: It has nested at 6,500 meters, higher than any other bird, and has been seen following climbers on Mount Everest at 8,200 meters.

8355.name: Mascarene Paradise-Flycatcher
8355.fact: It lacks the long tail of many paradise flycatchers, so look instead for the male's black head, chestnut back and bright blue bill.

8423.name: Pied Currawong
8423.fact: Flocks seem to play, with one bird perching atop a tall tree or spire while others swoop and dive trying to knock it off.

8470.name: Yucatan Jay
8470.fact: Juveniles have white heads and bodies that soon molt to black, but their yellow bills take into the second year to turn fully black.

8484.name: Plush-crested Jay
8484.fact: Raising chicks is a group effort, with several flock members bringing food and even getting rid of the nestlings' droppings.

8514.name: Gray Shrikethrush
8514.fact: One of Australasia's best-loved songbirds, it's common over most of Australia but missing from the driest inland deserts.

8575.name: Australian Magpie
8575.fact: Australian magpies can recognise at least 100 different people and may be less likely to swoop the ones they've befriended.

9083.name: Northern Cardinal
9083.fact: Defending his territory, a male may mistake his reflection in a shiny surface for an invading rival and fight it relentlessly.

9100.name: Song Sparrow
9100.fact: Its fear of hawks and owls seems to be instinctive, but a song sparrow has to learn to be afraid of cats.

9135.name: Chipping Sparrow
9135.fact: Before house sparrows were brought to North America, it lived in cities in large numbers, filling much the same niche they do now.

9176.name: White-crowned Sparrow
9176.fact: During migration it can stay half-awake for up to two weeks, a trick studied for keeping shift workers and truck drivers alert.

9183.name: Rufous-collared Sparrow
9183.fact: It's been seen picking termites out of spider webs, and its diverse vocalizations have been studied intensely since the 1970s.

9201.name: Reed Bunting
9201.fact: Males have a black head and throat set off by a white neck collar, while females are much duller with streaked brown heads.

9236.name: European Serin
9236.fact: Serinus, its Latin name, comes from serin, the French word for a canary, which may be a corruption of citrinus, Latin for lemon-colored.

9246.name: Island Canary
9246.fact: The bird is named after the Canary Islands, and the islands' name comes from the Latin for 'islands of dogs'.

9398.name: European Goldfinch
9398.fact: Because it eats thistle seeds, Christian symbolism links it to Christ's crown of thorns, as in Raphael's Madonna of the Goldfinch.

9420.name: Spotted Towhee
9420.fact: A big red-eyed sparrow with white-spotted wings, it has a habit of noisily rummaging through dry leaves on the ground for food.

9557.name: Green-headed Tanager
9557.fact: Its flashy blue-green colors camouflage it well among the leaves, so it's easy to miss even in the orchards and parks where it's common.

9607.name: Great-tailed Grackle
9607.fact: The Aztecs brought it to Tenochtitlan around 1500, probably for its iridescent feathers, and that's the earliest documented bird introduction in the Americas.

9612.name: Brown-capped Rosy-Finch
9612.fact: Its bill is yellow in winter and black in summer, and it breeds on mountain peaks in the central Rockies.

9744.name: Red-winged Blackbird
9744.fact: When researchers dyed males' red shoulder patches black, 64% lost their territories, compared with just 8% of the control birds.

9771.name: Pine Grosbeak
9771.fact: In poor fruit years it can move long distances south or downslope looking for food, and in winter it favors small fruits like rowan.

9864.name: Saffron Finch
9864.fact: Called the 'roof canary' in northern Venezuela, it usually nests in cavities like old rufous hornero nests or under house roofs.

9915.name: Summer Tanager
9915.fact: Mostly an insect eater, it's also been reported eating snails and slugs, and one tried to eat a green anole in Mississippi.

10070.name: Common Chaffinch
10070.fact: After farmers thresh their crops, it sometimes spends weeks picking grain out of the discarded chaff, which likely gave it its name.

10094.name: Dark-eyed Junco
10094.fact: A flock of these juncos is sometimes called a blizzard, which suits a bird whose scientific name means 'winter junco'.

10176.name: Green-backed Sparrow
10176.fact: Its nest is a dome on the ground with a side entrance, and nobody has yet studied what it eats.

10288.name: Blue-black Grassquit
10288.fact: Males are mostly black with a dark blue sheen and a white underwing patch that usually only shows in flight.

10293.name: Sayaca Tanager
10293.fact: It feeds on flowers, buds and insects, a mixed diet that's helped make it one of the most common city birds in southeastern Brazil.

10295.name: Blue-gray Tanager
10295.fact: It's more common in forest growing back on abandoned slash-and-burn plots than in primary forest that's never been cleared.

10325.name: Brewer's Blackbird
10325.fact: Often seen in parking lots, it's also been spotted following vehicles plowing fields to eat the churned-up insects.

10568.name: Black-throated Shrike-Tanager
10568.fact: Pairs almost always join mixed-species flocks, often acting as sentinels and snatching prey the flock stirs up in fast, acrobatic chases.

10607.name: Swallow Tanager
10607.fact: Turquoise-blue males wear a black mask over the face and throat, while females are mostly green.

11275.name: Rufous Hornero
11275.fact: Argentina's national bird sings in duets, each partner beating its wings in time with its trill, so the faster flapper is the male.

11901.name: Barn Swallow
11901.fact: The most widespread swallow in the world, it turns up on every continent, with strays reported even in Antarctica.

12037.name: Grey-backed Shrike
12037.fact: Harsh zzert-zzert calls mark its territory, but its breeding song is subdued and musical, with several minutes of mimicked bird calls.

12038.name: Red-backed Shrike
12038.fact: Frogs, lizards, small birds and large insects end up impaled on thorns or barbed wire in its larder, hence the nickname butcher bird.

12065.name: Superb Fairywren
12065.fact: Males pluck yellow petals and show them to females, sometimes in other territories and even outside the breeding season.

12133.name: Southern Emuwren
12133.fact: Named for its loosely barbed, emu-like tail feathers, it's among the smallest Australian birds, while the emu is the largest.

12580.name: Tūī
12580.fact: Looking black at first glance with a white tuft at its neck, it resembles a parson, and early colonists called it the parson bird.

12716.name: Eurasian Blackbird
12716.fact: Its name dates from when 'bird' meant a small bird and crows were 'fowl,' making it the only common black 'bird' in the British Isles.

12727.name: American Robin
12727.fact: With an estimated 370 million birds, it's the most abundant landbird in North America, ahead of red-winged blackbirds and starlings.

12748.name: Song Thrush
12748.fact: It's the emblem of West Bromwich Albion football club, because the pub the team once changed in kept a pet thrush in a cage.

12751.name: Austral Thrush
12751.fact: An accomplished mimic, it's known to imitate the songs of at least 12 other species, including songbirds and raptors.

12784.name: Red-capped Robin-Chat
12784.fact: Hippopotamus droppings sometimes go into its nest, an open cup both parents build from dead leaves, moss, lichen and bark.

12792.name: White-browed Robin-Chat
12792.fact: Usually sung at dawn and dusk, its song starts quietly and grows louder, with phrases like 'don't-you-do-it' sometimes repeated over ten times.

12810.name: Large Niltava
12810.fact: It lives in subtropical and tropical mountain forests from Nepal and Bhutan across to China, Vietnam, Malaysia and Indonesia.

12822.name: Northern Wheatear
12822.fact: The name wheatear is an altered, perhaps cleaned-up form of 'white-arse,' after its prominent white rump.

12908.name: Whinchat
12908.fact: Singing from fences, bushes and wires, the male often mixes phrases from at least 12 other bird species into his soft, crackly song.

12926.name: Collared Bush-Robin
12926.fact: Males of this Taiwan mountain endemic have a slate-black head, a white eyebrow and a rufous collar across the breast and back.

13082.name: Collared Palm-Thrush
13082.fact: A black line outlines its throat, and its pale eye and unspotted underparts set it apart from the similar spotted morning-thrush.

13094.name: European Robin
13094.fact: Territorial fights cause up to 10% of adult robin deaths in some areas, and robins have even been recorded attacking their own reflection.

13631.name: Black-crested Titmouse
13631.fact: It nests mostly in old woodpecker holes, whether in living or dead trees, fence posts or utility poles.

13688.name: Grey Wagtail
13688.fact: In display, the male flies a short way up, then flutters slowly down while giving a rapid series of high chipping notes.

13695.name: White Wagtail
13695.fact: The national bird of Latvia, it's adapted to towns by foraging for insects on paved areas like car parks.

13738.name: Berthelot's Pipit
13738.fact: Compared with a meadow pipit, it looks shorter-tailed and bigger-headed, and its 'schrip' call sounds like a yellow wagtail's.

13811.name: Taveta Golden-Weaver
13811.fact: Named after Kenya's Taveta region, it breeds in colonies, with males weaving oval nests onto reed or grass stems over water.

13851.name: Eurasian Tree Sparrow
13851.fact: Unlike other Old World sparrows, males and females look the same, with a chestnut crown and a black patch on each white cheek.

13853.name: Cape Sparrow
13853.fact: Also called the mossie, it appeared on South Africa's lowest-value coin from the 1923 farthing until the cent stopped being minted in 2002.

13858.name: House Sparrow
13858.fact: The male's black bib may signal his status, though studies have only firmly shown that it grows bigger with age.

13921.name: Scaly Weaver
13921.fact: Also called the scaly-feathered finch, it lives in Angola, Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

13956.name: Sociable Weaver
13956.fact: Its communal nest looks like a haystack in a tree and can house over 100 pairs, several generations at a time.

14005.name: Red-billed Quelea
14005.fact: Its flocks of millions feed like a rolling cloud, with birds at the back leapfrogging the whole group to fresh food at the front.

14110.name: Zebra Finch
14110.fact: More than half the birds in one experiment survived 513 days without being given any water to drink.

14168.name: Flame Robin
14168.fact: Look for males with a brilliant orange-red chest and a white forehead patch in the coolest parts of south-eastern Australia and Tasmania.

14175.name: Tomtit
14175.fact: Tomtits on the Snares Islands are entirely black and weigh about 20 grams, almost twice as much as birds on the main islands.

14497.name: Western Bowerbird
14497.fact: Males decorate their bowers with green and white objects like berries, shells and bones, and sometimes glass and gun casings.

14588.name: Common Bulbul
14588.fact: Its loud call goes 'doctor-quick doctor-quick be-quick be-quick', and its flight is bouncing and woodpecker-like.

14621.name: Light-vented Bulbul
14621.fact: A familiar bird of towns and urban parks, it may be Shanghai's third most common bird after tree sparrows and spotted doves.

14623.name: Yellow-vented Bulbul
14623.fact: At home around people, it even nests in gardens, building a loose cup that looks untidy outside but is neatly lined with plant fibers.

14939.name: Superb Starling
14939.fact: Check the eyes: pale creamy white on this one, red on the look-alike Hildebrandt's starling, which also lacks the white breast band.

14941.name: Meves's Starling
14941.fact: It can look plain black in dull light, and its longer, strongly graduated tail sets it apart from Burchell's starling.

14965.name: Asian Glossy Starling
14965.fact: Adults are glossy black and most have bright red eyes, while streaky juveniles have eyes of yellow, orange or pink.

15071.name: Bare-cheeked Babbler
15071.fact: Especially common in Etosha, it lives in noisy family groups of 6 to 12 birds that mob predators together.

15560.name: Red-billed Leiothrix
15560.fact: Cagebird keepers call it the Pekin robin or Japanese nightingale, though it's neither a robin nor a nightingale and isn't native to Japan.

16126.name: White-rumped Monjita
16126.fact: Perching tamely on fence posts and wires, it drops to the ground to grab insects, and parents even feed their young lizards.

16230.name: White-throated Spadebill
16230.fact: Only about 9 to 11 centimetres long, it has a large head with a bold face pattern, a stubby tail and a wide, flat bill.

16447.name: Vermilion Flycatcher
16447.fact: A favorite with birders, it's rarely kept in aviaries because captive males tend to lose their vermilion red, likely a matter of diet.

16462.name: Tropical Royal Flycatcher
16462.fact: Royal by name thanks to a striking, colorful crest, it rarely displays it except in courtship, after mating, while preening or when handled.

16787.name: Tropical Kingbird
16787.fact: The melancholicus in its name means melancholic, or bad-tempered, and it aggressively defends its territory even against frigatebirds, toucans and hawks.

16793.name: Fork-tailed Flycatcher
16793.fact: Adult males carry a tail two to three times longer than the rest of the bird, measured from bill to tail base.

16842.name: Social Flycatcher
16842.fact: It often nests near bee or wasp nests, building a bulky domed cup that can include cotton, paper and other human-made fibers.

16956.name: Great Kiskadee
16956.fact: Brazilians know it as bem-te-vi, 'I saw you well,' an echo of its exuberant BEE-tee-WEE call.

17013.name: Black Phoebe
17013.fact: Always near water, it cements its open cup nest in place with mud under a cliff or a bridge.

17278.name: Masked Water-Tyrant
17278.fact: Its range is split in two: eastern and southern Brazil, and a far-off area from southwestern Colombia through western Ecuador into Peru.

17383.name: Yucatan Vireo
17383.fact: In Belize it sings an evenly paced warble written as 'cheer up sweet' or 'cheer up why not sweet'.

17394.name: Eastern Warbling Vireo
17394.fact: The male helps incubate the eggs and may even sing from the nest, a deep cup hung from a branch or shrub.

17534.name: Bonin White-eye
17534.fact: Offered tinned peaches, it wouldn't touch them until it saw introduced warbling white-eyes eating them.

17638.name: American Three-toed Woodpecker
17638.fact: After a fire or flood it often moves into areas full of insect-infested trees, hunting wood-boring beetle larvae on the conifers.

17871.name: Great Spotted Woodpecker
17871.fact: As late as the early 1900s some thought its drumming might be vocal, and it wasn't proved purely mechanical until 1943.

17943.name: White-backed Woodpecker
17943.fact: Largest of the western Palearctic's spotted woodpeckers, it needs big tracts of mature deciduous forest with plenty of standing and fallen dead wood.

18014.name: White-spotted Woodpecker
18014.fact: It hammers beetle larvae out of trunks, saplings and even fence posts, and signals by tapping in groups of two to four.

18205.name: Red-bellied Woodpecker
18205.fact: To court a mate it'll drum on hollow trees, and in towns on aluminum roofs, metal gutters and even transformer boxes.

18584.name: Collared Aracari
18584.fact: As many as seven may share a single cavity to roost overnight, and they usually travel in groups of about six to fifteen.

18880.name: Blue-winged Parrot
18880.fact: It's one of only three parrots that migrate over the sea every year, with many breeding in Tasmania and wintering on the mainland.

18911.name: Rose-ringed Parakeet
18911.fact: Escaped pets have colonised cities in northern and western Europe, coping with low winter temperatures far from their tropical native range.

18921.name: Crimson Rosella
18921.fact: In the breeding season, females often raid other rosellas' nests and destroy the eggs, the most common reason an egg fails to hatch.

18938.name: Hyacinth Macaw
18938.fact: Its beak can crack coconuts, yet acuri palm nuts are so hard that it only eats them once they've passed through cattle.

19050.name: Brown-headed Parrot
19050.fact: The cryptoxanthus in its scientific name comes from Greek words for 'hidden yellow', after the bright yellow feathers under its wings.

19073.name: Lilian's Lovebird
19073.fact: The smallest parrot on mainland Africa, it's often mistaken for Fischer's lovebird, which is slightly larger, with a blue rump.

19975.name: Burrowing Owl
19975.fact: Despite the name, it rarely digs its own burrow, moving instead into old ones dug by prairie dogs, ground squirrels, badgers or foxes.

20044.name: Great Horned Owl
20044.fact: A poor sense of smell lets it routinely attack skunks with impunity, and its nests often reek of skunk.

20500.name: Southern Cassowary
20500.fact: Of 150 attacks on people in a 2003 study, three in four came from birds people had fed, and only one was fatal.

20526.name: Common Ostrich
20526.fact: Its eyes are the largest of any land vertebrate, 50 millimetres across, which helps it spot predators at a great distance.

20637.name: Elegant Crested-Tinamou
20637.fact: Its flights cover only about 500 meters, and a botched takeoff can end in a fatal crash into a branch or wire.

20969.name: Common Hoopoe
20969.fact: Its feathered crown can be raised or lowered at will, and the name hoopoe imitates the bird's call.

21614.name: Taiwan Common Toad
21614.fact: In one study, toads from a temperate area could breed all year, but subtropical ones bred only in the cooler months, September to March.

22075.name: Painted Trilling Frog
22075.fact: When threatened, it sometimes rears up on all its legs and inflates its body to look bigger to predators.

23006.name: Santa Catarina Tree Toad
23006.fact: Males measure about 25 to 28 mm from snout to vent, with a brown or gray back marked with stripes and a white belly.

23027.name: Rock River Frog
23027.fact: This rock-loving frog can even live on rocky sea shores, where it forages in the intertidal zone.

23366.name: Angolan Reed Frog
23366.fact: Extremely abundant, it readily colonizes newly created water bodies and even turns up in towns and gardens.

24259.name: Pacific chorus frog
24259.fact: Sensing food nearby, it often twitches a toe to lure the prey within easy reach of its tongue.

24495.name: European Fire-Bellied Toad
24495.fact: When threatened it lifts its arms, sometimes flipping over, to flash its black-mottled red belly and warn predators it's toxic.

25588.name: Columbia Spotted Frog
25588.fact: Females lay masses of up to 1,300 eggs that swell to softball size and float free instead of clinging to plants.

25591.name: European Common Frog
25591.fact: In the Alps it can stay in hibernation until early June, getting all the oxygen it needs through its skin.

26068.name: Saltwater Crocodile
26068.fact: Its broad body had early observers taking it for an alligator, which is why northern Australia's Alligator Rivers carry the wrong reptile's name.

26079.name: Freshwater Crocodile
26079.fact: A slender snout sets it apart from the saltwater crocodile, and it can live where its bigger relative can't, like above Kakadu's escarpment.

26159.name: American Alligator
26159.fact: When water starts to freeze, it pokes its snout through the surface to breathe above the ice and can stay that way for days.

26567.name: Dark-eared Tree Frog
26567.fact: Found even in some large cities, it lays its eggs in foam nests on leaves or twigs that hang over ponds and ditches.

26747.name: Northwestern Salamander
26747.fact: Gilled adults get more common with altitude, so lowland adults almost all live on land while most at very high elevations keep their gills.

27125.name: Blue Ridge Two-lined Salamander
27125.fact: Bright yellow to orange, it has two black lines along its back that usually break into dots around the middle of its long tail.

27136.name: Shenandoah Salamander
27136.fact: Found only on the north-facing talus slopes of Hawksbill, The Pinnacles and Stony Man in Shenandoah National Park.

27188.name: White-spotted Slimy Salamander
27188.fact: Touch it and it freezes in place, and glands on its back release a sticky, noxious substance to deter predators.

27411.name: Pygmy Salamander
27411.fact: Just 35 to 44 millimetres long, it's among the smallest salamanders in the world and has no free-living larval stage.

27413.name: Seal Salamander
27413.fact: The monticola in its scientific name is Latin for 'mountaineer' or 'highlander', after the high elevations where it's commonly found.

27705.name: Danube Crested Newt
27705.fact: The smallest crested newt, it has a slender swimmer's body built on 16 or 17 rib-bearing vertebrae, more than any other crested newt.

29044.name: Gopher Snake
29044.fact: When threatened it puffs up, coils like a rattlesnake and vibrates its tail, but it often strikes with its mouth closed.

30737.name: Panamint Rattlesnake
30737.fact: Also called the tiger rattlesnake, it gives birth to live young in July and August, each about 25 centimetres long.

30901.name: Meadow Viper
30901.fact: Europe's smallest viper is also its most threatened snake, at risk from grazing, mowing, fire and illegal collecting.

30983.name: Pygmy Rattlesnake
30983.fact: North America's smallest rattlesnake has a rattle so tiny that its buzz can only be heard from a few feet away.

30996.name: Brown spotted pitviper
30996.fact: Grayish or olive brown with big black-edged brown blotches, it ranges from northeastern India to Taiwan and has been introduced to Okinawa.

31127.name: Namib Rock Agama
31127.fact: Orange-and-blue males court the dappled, checkered females by running in circles around them while bobbing their heads.

31132.name: Mwanza Flat-headed Rock Agama
31132.fact: Males wear Spider-Man colors, a red or violet head and shoulders on a dark blue body, which has made the lizard a fashionable pet.

31150.name: Southern Rock Agama
31150.fact: Approached by a predator, a breeding male presses flat against the rock and swaps his bright blue head for duller camouflage colors.

31192.name: Orange-winged Flying Lizard
31192.fact: Gliding from tree to tree on black-spotted wings, the male also has a throat flap often twice as long as its head.

31230.name: Central Netted Dragon
31230.fact: About a quarter of its wild diet is plants, like hogweed and daisy flowers, making it one of Australia's most herbivorous desert lizards.

31271.name: Forest Garden Lizard
31271.fact: Look for three separate small clusters of spines on each side of its head, one behind the brow and two above the eardrum.

31302.name: Green Crested Lizard
31302.fact: This bright green lizard turns darker brown when threatened, and its very long, thin tail makes up three quarters of its length.

31648.name: Blue-eyed Anglehead Lizard
31648.fact: Only males have the blue eyes in its name, while females have brown ones.

31651.name: Malayan Crested Lizard
31651.fact: Known as the giant forest dragon or great anglehead lizard, it lives in Thailand, Myanmar, Vietnam, Malaysia and Indonesia.

32837.name: Johnston's Chameleon
32837.fact: Only adult males grow three ringed horns, and they're fiercely territorial, fighting other males with horns and bites.

33004.name: Panther Chameleon
33004.fact: Its color depends on where it lives, with panther chameleons from Nosy Be typically blue and those from Maroantsetra mostly red.

33016.name: Carpet Chameleon
33016.fact: Fast-maturing and short-lived, it can breed about three months after hatching but rarely if ever lives past three years.

33118.name: Brown Basilisk
33118.fact: Smaller ones can sprint about 10 to 20 meters across water without sinking, opening flaps on their hind feet for extra surface area.

34033.name: Ornate Day Gecko
34033.fact: In 2014 five of these geckos were sent to space for a microgravity breeding test, and died after their heating system failed.

34042.name: Striped Day Gecko
34042.fact: More colorful than the females, males are green with red splotches on the head and lower back and a dark band down each side.

34050.name: Gold Dust Day Gecko
34050.fact: Gold speckles on the neck and upper back mark it out, and since 1999 one has been GEICO's talking mascot.

35303.name: Black Spiny-tailed Iguana
35303.fact: The Guinness Book of World Records lists it as the world's fastest lizard, with a top sprint speed of 34.6 kilometers per hour.

35347.name: Marine Iguana
35347.fact: During El Niño food shortages, it can shrink by up to a fifth of its length, then grow back when the algae return.

35453.name: Viviparous Lizard
35453.fact: No other land reptile lives farther north, and in especially cold winters it can freeze completely and thaw out two months later.

35474.name: Madeira Lizard
35474.fact: Ships trading between Madeira and the Azores accidentally carried it across, and it now lives wild in the Azores too.

35519.name: Large Psammodromus
35519.fact: Found in southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa, it also goes by the name Algerian psammodromus.

35700.name: Cretan Wall Lizard
35700.fact: You'll only find this wall lizard on Crete and the satellite islands around it, nowhere else in the world.

35912.name: Sand Lizard
35912.fact: Rematches between rival males tend to be much shorter than their first fight, likely because they recognize each other and can predict the outcome.

35964.name: Iberian Rock Lizard
35964.fact: Green spreads over it with age, belly first and then the back, and females tend to mate with the greener males.

35995.name: Tenerife Lizard
35995.fact: A fruit, flower and nectar eater, it's a major pollinator and seed disperser, and sometimes a nuisance in vineyards and orchards.

36080.name: Zebra-tailed Lizard
36080.fact: In the hottest part of the day, it may stand on two legs, then switch to the other two in a kind of dance.

36094.name: Common Side-blotched Lizard
36094.fact: In its rock-paper-scissors mating game, yellow-throated males mimic females to sneak matings from the harems of big orange-throated males.

36142.name: Eastern Fence Lizard
36142.fact: It twitches to throw off attacking fire ants before fleeing, and in some regions it has evolved longer legs to escape them.

36189.name: Crevice Spiny Lizard
36189.fact: Shy and nervous, it flees up a rock face or into a crevice when approached, and females bear up to 11 young in midsummer.

36204.name: Western Fence Lizard
36204.fact: Ticks carrying Lyme disease that feed on it come away clean, because a protein in its blood kills the bacterium in their gut.

36217.name: Canyon Lizard
36217.fact: It lives on the rock faces of canyon walls, sheltering in crevices, and its gray, tan or reddish-brown back matches the rock.

36339.name: Keeled Earless Lizard
36339.fact: Named for the keeled scales on its back, it's perhaps most common in the loose, shifting sands of beaches and barrier islands.

36514.name: Green Anole
36514.fact: Its ancestors crossed the sea from Cuba to the southern United States, a rare case of an island lizard colonizing a mainland.

36643.name: Amazon Green Anole
36643.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its common names and the countries it lives in, and the Anolis article has nothing beyond taxonomy that holds for every anole.

38008.name: Common Sun Skink
38008.fact: First spotted in Taiwan in 1992, it has spread through the island's western lowlands but its poor cold tolerance keeps it below 500 meters.

38066.name: Karasburg Tree Skink
38066.fact: The Trachylepis in its scientific name means 'rough-scaled', since most Trachylepis skinks have faint ridges on smooth-looking back scales.

38382.name: Bojer's Skink
38382.fact: Invasive Asian house shrews helped drive its decline, and the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation has since eradicated them from its habitat.

38492.name: Yellow-bellied Water Skink
38492.fact: Look for it basking on waterside logs and rocks, as it prefers rocky places near creeks, rivers, bogs and swamps.

38992.name: Western Collared Spiny Lizard
38992.fact: As in all Tropidurus lizards, males and females are marked differently, and the male is usually much larger and more brightly colored.

39122.name: Austral Smooth-throated lizard
39122.fact: One of the world's southernmost lizards, it lives on Patagonia's windswept steppe and gives birth to live young, usually three to five.

39174.name: Black-faced Smooth-throated Lizard
39174.why: Its Wikipedia article says only that it's a lizard found in Argentina, and the Liolaemus article covers just the whole group's range, size and diet.

39469.name: Lace Monitor
39469.fact: Mitochondrial DNA shows its closest relative is the Komodo dragon, and the two lineages split more than 11 million years ago.

39484.name: Desert Night Lizard
39484.fact: Unusually for a lizard, a father, mother and young live together as a family, and the young may stay for years.

39659.name: Green Sea Turtle
39659.fact: The green in its name comes from the fat under its shell, colored by a seagrass diet, while the shell itself is olive to black.

39782.name: Pond Slider
39782.fact: The 'slider' in its name comes from how basking groups scramble off logs and shoot back into the water when they sense danger.

39814.name: Common Box Turtle
39814.fact: When it overheats, it smears saliva on its legs and head, and may even urinate on its hind legs to cool off.

39824.name: Florida Red-bellied Cooter
39824.fact: Known for sometimes laying its eggs in alligator nest mounds, it has a red-tinged belly and two toothlike cusps on its upper beak.

40232.name: Tasmanian Devil
40232.fact: Tasmania's early explorers heard its far-carrying screeches at night before they ever saw one, and nicknamed it 'Beelzebub's pup'.

40579.name: Common Thick-thumbed Bat
40579.fact: Look for thick white or pink pads at the base of its thumbs, and by day it roosts in dead bamboo stalks or banana leaves.

40872.name: Bonin Flying-fox
40872.fact: One of the northernmost flying foxes, it spends winter days in colonies of up to 100, packed into a ball to keep warm.

41505.name: White-beaked Dolphin
41505.fact: With up to 92 vertebrae, it has more than any other oceanic dolphin, and it often rides the bow waves of fast boats.

41550.name: Common Minke Whale
41550.fact: The name's origin is murky, but one story points to Meincke, a German laborer who once mistook a school of them for blue whales.

41562.name: Fin Whale
41562.fact: Second only to the blue whale in length, it's often seen in pods of 6 to 10 that communicate at 16 to 40 hertz.

41566.name: Humpback Whale
41566.fact: Its flippers are each about a third of its body length, and it usually uses bubbles to catch krill and small fish.

41638.name: American Black Bear
41638.fact: In experiments, black bears learned to tell colors apart faster than chimpanzees and just as fast as domestic dogs.

41663.name: Common Raccoon
41663.fact: To climb down a tree headfirst, an unusual skill for a mammal its size, it rotates its hind feet so they point backwards.

41670.name: South American Coati
41670.fact: Solitary males were once thought to be a separate species, called coatimundis, because they live so differently from the female bands.

41702.name: Harp Seal
41702.fact: Pups wear a white coat for their first two to three weeks, and the black harp pattern doesn't show until they near maturity.

41720.name: Bearded Seal
41720.fact: In the breeding season males sing a long, warbling trill that ends in a moan and can be heard over 30 km away underwater.

41752.name: Long-nosed Fur Seal
41752.fact: It dives deeper and longer than any other fur seal, with males reaching about 380 meters for around 15 minutes.

41761.name: South American Sea Lion
41761.fact: At Península Valdés, orcas will beach themselves to grab these sea lions near the shore.

41766.name: Walrus
41766.fact: An air sac under its throat works like a flotation bubble, letting it bob upright in the water and sleep.

41845.name: Giant Otter
41845.fact: Known in Brazil as the water jaguar, it's the noisiest otter, and each family has its own audio signature.

41886.name: Spotted Hyena
41886.fact: The pitch of its famous laugh gives away a hyena's age, while the notes it uses signal its social rank.

41921.name: Banded Mongoose
41921.fact: With nowhere to hide from predators like African wild dogs, a group lies piled together with heads facing out and up.

41955.name: Cheetah
41955.fact: Cheetahs vary so little genetically that skin grafts swapped between unrelated animals are accepted and heal, as if they shared the same genes.

41964.name: Lion
41964.fact: In Ngorongoro Crater, lions live largely on kills stolen from hyenas, but in Botswana's Chobe National Park the hyenas do the stealing.

41967.name: Tiger
41967.fact: Besides roaring, tigers make a deer-like 'pok' sound, most often at kills, for reasons that are still unknown.

42051.name: Coyote
42051.fact: Coyotes sometimes team up with American badgers to dig out rodents, and some have been seen resting their heads on their badger partners.

42076.name: Gray Fox
42076.fact: Unlike the red fox, it has oval pupils instead of slits and no black stockings, plus a black stripe down its tail.

42077.name: Island Fox
42077.fact: North America's smallest fox, it probably reached the Channel Islands with the help of early humans around 7,000 years ago.

42122.name: Common Warthog
42122.fact: It kneels on calloused pads on its wrists to graze, and those pads start forming before it's even born.

42149.name: Common Hippopotamus
42149.fact: For an animal that spends most of the day in water, it may not swim at all, walking or bouncing along the bottom instead.

42220.name: Mule Deer
42220.fact: Named for its big, mule-like ears, it's often seen stotting, with all four feet coming down together.

42223.name: White-tailed Deer
42223.fact: Bambi is a roe deer in the original novel, but Disney's 1942 film made him a white-tailed deer.

42240.name: Guanaco
42240.fact: A teaspoon of guanaco blood holds about 68 million red blood cells, four times a human's, which helps the animal survive at high altitude.

42278.name: Impala
42278.fact: Seemingly the only hoofed mammal that grooms itself and others, it combs ticks from a partner's head and neck with its lower front teeth.

42283.name: Springbok
42283.fact: During droughts, millions of migrating springbok once formed herds hundreds of kilometers long that could take several days to pass a town.

42308.name: Gemsbok
42308.fact: New Mexico released 93 gemsbok between 1969 and 1977, and about 3,000 now live in the desert around the White Sands Missile Range.

42326.name: Puku
42326.fact: When scared, it repeats a shrill whistle, and in the rainy season female herds band together, often around 50 strong, for safety.

42329.name: Lechwe
42329.fact: Coated in a water-repellent substance, its legs let it run fast through the knee-deep water it uses for protection from predators.

42342.name: Nyala
42342.fact: Males and females look more different than in any other spiral-horned antelope, the males slate gray and horned, the females rusty brown and striped.

42347.name: Northern Chamois
42347.fact: Chamois tend to watch for danger from below, so a hunter stalking them from above is less likely to be spotted.

42390.name: Thinhorn Sheep
42390.fact: Denali National Park and Preserve was created in 1917 to protect these sheep from overhunting, and they're still often seen there.

42405.name: African Buffalo
42405.fact: Herds decide where to eat or drink by 'voting', with females standing up before dusk to point in a particular direction.

42475.name: Tailless Tenrec
42475.fact: The first tropical mammal observed to hibernate, it can go up to nine months at a time without waking.

42881.name: Western Grey Kangaroo
42881.fact: Mature males have a distinctive curry-like smell, which earned the species its nickname, 'stinker'.

42970.name: Rufous-bellied Pademelon
42970.fact: It's been reported standing upright to yank up clumps of grass and throw them against its chest, possibly as a signal.

42983.name: Koala
42983.fact: Its eucalyptus diet is low in nutrition and toxic enough to deter most other mammals, and it sleeps up to twenty hours a day.

43009.name: Bare-nosed Wombat
43009.fact: Besides leaving cube-shaped dung, it digs burrows up to 20 meters long that echidnas, wallabies, birds and even koalas also use.

43048.name: Northern White-breasted Hedgehog
43048.fact: Size follows climate in this hedgehog: it grows larger in southern Europe than in the north, and smaller where summers are wetter.

43086.name: Rock Hyrax
43086.fact: Perfumers steep its hyraceum, a sticky mass of dung and urine used in South African folk medicine, in alcohol to make a natural musk.

43111.name: Eastern Cottontail
43111.fact: Originally absent from New England, it was introduced there and now competes with the native New England cottontail.

43128.name: Brown Hare
43128.fact: In spring 'boxing' bouts, it's sometimes a female hitting a male, to show she isn't ready to mate or to test his determination.

43188.name: American Pika
43188.fact: Active by day, it stores plants in 'haypiles' to last the winter and calls out to warn of approaching predators.

43197.name: Collared Pika
43197.fact: It spends much of the summer stacking plants into haypiles for winter, but some have been seen eating dead birds for fat and protein.

43335.name: Plains Zebra
43335.fact: The largest wild zebra herd outside Africa roams San Simeon, California, descended from animals left behind when Hearst Castle's private zoo closed.

43345.name: Indian Rhinoceros
43345.fact: When fighting, it inflicts wounds mostly with its lower incisors and uses its horn less often than African rhinos do.

43410.name: Black-faced Spider Monkey
43410.fact: Almost thumbless, with a gripping tail up to a meter long, it moves through the trees with an agility only Asia's gibbons can match.

43426.name: Black-capped Squirrel Monkey
43426.fact: Females run its big troops and push the males out to the edges, unlike the common squirrel monkey, whose troops are male-dominated.

43436.name: Mantled Howler Monkey
43436.fact: Disturb one and it'll often show its irritation by urinating or defecating on you, with good aim from high in the trees.

43450.name: Formosan Rock Macaque
43450.fact: Taiwan's only native primate apart from people, it screams when outsiders come near its troop.

43460.name: Rhesus Macaque
43460.fact: In 1938 a Florida tour boat operator released some at Silver Springs to live on a river island, not realizing they're strong swimmers.

43486.name: Blue Monkey
43486.fact: It often teams up with red-tailed monkeys for extra protection, and the two species even groom each other.

43502.name: Maroon Leaf Monkey
43502.fact: It eats topsoil from termite mounds, which is high in calcium and magnesium, to keep its diet balanced.

43613.name: Common Brown Lemur
43613.fact: Mostly active by day, it may carry on into the night, especially under a full moon or in the dry season.

43617.name: Ring-tailed Lemur
43617.fact: Rival males hold stink fights, soaking their tails in scent from glands on their arms and waving them at each other.

43694.name: African Savanna Elephant
43694.fact: A lower-ranking elephant greets its superior by putting the tip of its trunk into the other's mouth.

43712.name: Central American Agouti
43712.fact: Agoutis placed fourth for sense of smell in an analysis of 240 species, beating dogs, which came out only average.

43715.name: Black Agouti
43715.fact: Apart from its main range in the northwestern Amazon, there's a separate population in the Magdalena River valley of northern Colombia.

45941.name: Northern Gray-bellied Squirrel
45941.fact: True to its name, its belly is usually gray, while its back is gray, yellowish-olive or reddish depending on subspecies and season.

45949.name: Variable Squirrel
45949.fact: Living up to the name variable squirrel, it can be whitish, blackish or reddish all over, depending on the subspecies.

45952.name: Pallas' Squirrel
45952.fact: It's been seen mobbing tree-climbing snakes, and females protecting their young are especially likely to join in.

45955.name: Prevost's Squirrel
45955.fact: Durians are on its menu, and by carrying fruit far from the tree before dropping the seeds, it helps those plants survive.

46017.name: Eastern Gray Squirrel
46017.fact: If it feels watched, it fakes burying its food, keeping the morsel in its mouth while covering up an empty hole.

46086.name: Yellow-bellied Marmot
46086.fact: Notorious for seeking sweet-smelling radiator fluid, some have ridden out of the Sierra under car hoods to the San Francisco Bay Area.

46087.name: Hoary Marmot
46087.fact: Whistler, British Columbia, once called London Mountain, was renamed after this marmot, nicknamed 'the whistler' for its high-pitched alarm call.

46093.name: Olympic Marmot
46093.fact: Found only on Washington's Olympic Peninsula, this cat-sized marmot became the state's official endemic mammal in 2009.

46259.name: Douglas's Squirrel
46259.fact: Native Americans of the Kings River called it the 'Pillillooeet', copying the sound of its alarm call.

47067.name: Brown-throated Three-toed Sloth
47067.fact: Algae grow in tiny cracks in its coarse hairs, sometimes giving it a greenish tint, and its neck can turn up to 270 degrees.

47219.name: Western Honey Bee
47219.fact: One of the first domesticated insects, it now lives on every continent except Antarctica, with human help.

47571.name: European aspen
47571.fact: Flattened leaf stalks make its leaves tremble in even a slight breeze, which is where the scientific name tremula comes from.

47602.name: common dandelion
47602.fact: Each yellow flower head turns into a round 'clock' or 'blowball' of silver-tufted fruit that scatters on the wind.

47776.name: Pacific Banana Slug
47776.fact: Though it tends to avoid slime trails, even its own, it can find its way back to the same spot after long periods away.

47914.name: Pandorus Sphinx
47914.fact: Its caterpillars can pull the head and first two body segments back into the third, and they feed on grape and Virginia creeper.

48302.name: Atlantic Horseshoe Crab
48302.fact: Cape Cod once offered five cents for every dead horseshoe crab turned in, over a mistaken belief that they hurt fisheries.

48328.name: Common Moon Jelly
48328.fact: You can spot it by the four horseshoe-shaped gonads showing through the top of its almost entirely translucent bell.

48342.name: Purple Shore Crab
48342.fact: Check the claws: its white-tipped pincers carry purple or red spots, which the similar lined shore crab lacks.

48484.name: Asian Lady Beetle
48484.fact: Called the Halloween beetle in parts of North America, it often invades homes in October to spend the winter.

48655.name: California Seahare
48655.fact: Of the two inks it can release, reddish-purple and milky white, the milky one makes predators attack the cloud as if it were food.

48662.name: Monarch
48662.fact: Eastern monarchs fly thousands of miles south to Florida and Mexico each fall, and it takes several generations to return north in spring.

48987.name: Convergent Lady Beetle
48987.fact: In the western United States, it may spend up to nine months dormant in large groups in mountain valleys.

49133.name: Red Admiral
49133.fact: Unusually calm, it often lets people get very close and will even land on them to use as a perch.

49150.name: Gulf Fritillary
49150.fact: Its species name, vanillae, comes from a 1705 painting showing it on a vanilla orchid, a plant its caterpillars don't actually use.

49336.name: Death Valley Pupfish
49336.fact: It can withstand water four times saltier than the ocean and anywhere from freezing up to 116°F, conditions that would kill other fish.

49348.name: White-lined Sphinx
49348.fact: Some Native Americans skewered and roasted its caterpillars, which have almost as much fat as hamburger meat but nearly a third less saturated fat.

49540.name: Spinybacked Orbweaver
49540.fact: Females carry six spine-like points on the abdomen, and it keeps an unusual 19-hour wake-sleep cycle.

49699.name: Ochre Sea Star
49699.fact: Remove it from a stretch of shore and California mussels take over almost completely, which is why it's called a keystone species.

49761.name: White Peacock
49761.fact: Males stake out a territory about 15 meters across that holds caterpillar food plants and aggressively defend it from other insects.

50238.name: Carpet Python
50238.fact: After laying 10 to 50 eggs, the female coils around them, warming them with heat from her own muscle contractions.

50336.name: Malachite
50336.fact: Adults feed on nectar, rotting fruit, dead animals and bat dung, and the green chrysalis has sharp gold spines that can puncture predators.

50880.name: Lorquin's Admiral
50880.fact: Fiercely territorial, it will attack anything that strays into its patch, even large birds.

51110.name: Eastern Carpenter Bee
51110.fact: Its sharp, wedge-shaped mouthparts slit the side of flower tubes so it can reach the nectar from outside.

51275.name: Forest Bug
51275.fact: Look for the pair of points jutting forward from its shoulders, and its legs are usually red-brown or bright orange.

51566.name: Blue Pansy
51566.fact: Its looks depend on temperature, since cold-shocked caterpillars grow into adults with fewer eyespots and heat-shocked pupae come out less blue.

51588.name: Common Mormon Swallowtail
51588.fact: Named in India with a nod to Mormon polygamy, it has three different forms of female, two of which mimic poisonous rose swallowtails.

51659.name: Giant Green Anemone
51659.fact: Detached mussels seem to be its main food, but in rare cases it has engulfed seabirds, and nobody knows if they were alive.

51702.name: Seven-spotted Lady Beetle
51702.fact: Short of aphids, it survives on pollen, nectar, thrips and whitefly, but it can't reproduce in the meantime.

51736.name: small balsam
51736.fact: Ripe seed pods explode when touched and fling the seeds widely, which is why it's also called small-flowered touch-me-not.

51781.name: Cinnabar moth
51781.fact: Its caterpillars eat ragwort so greedily that big groups can strip whole patches bare, and when food runs short they may turn cannibal.

51875.name: Red Clover
51875.fact: A pale crescent marks the outer half of each leaflet, and its dark pink flowers are mostly visited by bumblebees.

51940.name: Asian House Gecko
51940.fact: At night it climbs house walls after insects drawn to porch lights, and its chirping makes it easy to recognize.

52413.name: Poplar Admiral
52413.fact: Skipping flowers altogether, it's drawn to the smell of carrion and dung and sips minerals from tree sap, soil and sweat.

52460.name: Houndfish
52460.fact: Feared by fishermen, it can leap from the water when frightened or drawn to lights and stab people with its beak.

52490.name: Tapered Drone Fly
52490.fact: Check the feet: on the front and middle legs they're entirely yellow, and males have a triangular abdomen, females a squarish one.

52555.name: Chameleon Wrasse
52555.why: No Wikipedia article of its own, and the Halichoeres article has nothing that holds for every wrasse in it.

52564.name: Aggregating Anemone
52564.fact: Rival clone colonies fight with special stinging tentacles, and a scout polyp that comes home badly stung may be attacked by its own clonemates.

52592.name: Speckled Wood
52592.fact: Northern speckled woods are bigger and darker than southern ones, with longer forewings that help them handle cooler temperatures.

52764.name: common selfheal
52764.fact: The names self-heal and heal-all come from its uses in traditional medicine, and the Quileute put its juice on boils.

52821.name: common yarrow
52821.fact: Starlings and other cavity-nesting birds line their nests with it, and legend says Achilles carried it to treat his army's battle wounds.

52943.name: White-striped Black
52943.fact: Its caterpillars feed on Impatiens plants, and adults are on the wing from April to September, from Alaska to Newfoundland and Labrador.

54064.name: Eastern Comma
54064.fact: This butterfly seldom visits flowers, feeding instead on sap, rotting fruit, dung and minerals it sips from puddles.

54087.name: Green-veined White
54087.fact: Males give off a sex pheromone people can actually smell, citral, the compound that gives lemon peel oil its flavor.

54468.name: Small Tortoiseshell
54468.fact: With its wings shut, it looks like a leaf, and birds may take up to 30 minutes to spot one on the ground.

54692.name: Wire Rush
54692.fact: Its scientific name translates as 'small tangle-foot', and its stems stand upright when short but lie along the ground once tall.

54699.name: Mānuka
54699.fact: The easiest way to tell it from kānuka is to feel the leaves: mānuka's are prickly, while kānuka's are soft.

54869.name: Terai Sacred Langur
54869.fact: A leaf-eater of the sal forest canopy, it has also been seen feeding in orchards and crop fields outside Rajaji National Park.

55376.name: Whitebar Surgeonfish
55376.fact: A dark-edged whitish band runs from its dorsal fin across the gill cover, and it grazes algae in small groups among surge-zone boulders.

55625.name: Common Darter
55625.fact: One of the easiest dragonflies to photograph, it keeps coming back to the same sunny perch, so you can predict where it'll land.

55626.name: Small White
55626.fact: Accidentally introduced to Quebec around 1860, it spread rapidly across North America, and its caterpillar is a pest of cabbage, kale and broccoli.

55637.name: Common Carder Bumble Bee
55637.fact: Queens prefer to build in old mouse nests, shaping moss and grass into a small hollow ball partly bonded with wax.

55640.name: Holly Blue
55640.fact: Holly blue numbers boom and crash in cycles that appear driven by an ichneumon wasp that lays eggs inside the caterpillars.

55641.name: Common Blue
55641.fact: Females are usually brown, but colder temperatures while they develop make them bluer, and in Ireland and Scotland their upperwings can be mostly blue.

55655.name: Small Copper
55655.fact: Males vigorously defend small territories against rivals or any passing insect, and even a big bird's shadow overhead can set one off.

55719.name: Common Drone Fly
55719.fact: Its aquatic larva, the rat-tailed maggot, breathes through a tail-like siphon that can be several times its body length.

55745.name: white clover
55745.fact: Clover sampled in 160 cities made more cyanide the farther it grew from downtown, suggesting it's adapting to city life.

55990.name: Common Wall Lizard
55990.fact: Cincinnati calls it the Lazarus lizard because a boy whose family owned the Lazarus department stores released about 10 there around 1950.

56225.name: European Comma
56225.fact: Its caterpillar wears a white stripe that mimics a bird dropping, and folded up, the adult looks like a dead leaf.

56529.name: Old World Swallowtail
56529.fact: Its caterpillar starts out looking like a bird dropping and can push out a smelly orange fork that deters insects but not birds.

56832.name: Mourning Cloak
56832.fact: Adults live 11 to 12 months, one of the longest lifespans of any butterfly, and it's Montana's state insect.

56916.name: Marsh Pennywort
56916.fact: Smelling faintly of carrot, it has round, shield-shaped leaves whose stalks attach in the middle of the underside.

57333.name: Mexican Hogfish
57333.fact: Starting life as a female, it later becomes a male, and large males sport a pronounced hump between the eyes.

57458.name: Chalk-fronted Corporal
57458.fact: Unusually sociable for a dragonfly, it often perches in groups and readily approaches people to eat the mosquitoes and biting flies they attract.

57516.name: Buff-tailed Bumble Bee
57516.fact: Used for greenhouse pollination, it's escaped and become invasive in places like Japan, Chile, Argentina and Tasmania.

58518.name: Common Roadside-Skipper
58518.fact: Adults favor low-growing blue flowers like verbena and selfheal, while the caterpillars eat grasses such as bluegrass and Bermuda grass.

58523.name: Black Swallowtail
58523.fact: When threatened, its caterpillar pushes out an orange forked gland that looks like a snake's tongue and gives off a foul smell.

58611.name: Ruddy Bowfin
58611.fact: Breaking the surface to gulp air, it can survive low-oxygen water that would kill most other fish.

59202.name: Yellow-legged Gull
59202.fact: When Italy's 2020 lockdown cut off their food scraps, Rome's yellow-legged gulls turned to hunting prey as large as rats and rock doves.

59399.name: Pelican's-foot
59399.fact: The flared lip of its adult shell has three or four points like a pelican's webbed foot, and empty shells sometimes wash ashore.

59588.name: Brimstone Moth
59588.fact: Its bright yellow wings, with small brown patches along the front edge of each forewing, make it unmistakable in its range.

60342.name: Western Ribbon Snake
60342.fact: A whitish, unmarked upper lip stands out against the dark head, and the very long tail makes up about a third of its length.

60551.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
60551.fact: John White drew one on Sir Walter Raleigh's 1587 expedition to Virginia, the first known drawing of a North American butterfly.

60607.name: Red-spotted Admiral
60607.fact: Southern populations lack the white wing band of northern ones and instead mimic the poisonous pipevine swallowtail, with lots of hybrids where they meet.

61495.name: Eastern Pondhawk
61495.fact: Males start out bright green like the females, then shift to blue and finally a powdery bluish-gray over their adult lives.

61523.name: Roman Snail
61523.fact: Eaten by the ancient Romans and prized in French cooking as escargot, it's hard to farm and rarely raised commercially.

61608.name: Sand Hammertail
61608.fact: A robber fly that hunts tiger beetles, including the hairy-necked tiger beetle and the northeastern beach tiger beetle.

61781.name: Large Skipper
61781.fact: Its caterpillar curls a leaf up with silk for a shelter, then hibernates half-grown and carries on feeding in spring.

61918.name: Magpie Moth
61918.fact: Research on this moth, which comes in many different forms, is what first revealed sex-linked traits.

62393.name: Jonah Crab
62393.fact: Fishermen once threw it back as a pest that stole bait from lobster traps, but US landings topped 17 million pounds in 2014.

62426.name: Ringlet
62426.fact: Newly emerged, it looks velvety and almost black, with a white fringe edging its wings.

62429.name: Gatekeeper
62429.fact: To tell it from the meadow brown, look for wings held open at rest and double pupils in the eyespots.

62470.name: Leopard Slug
62470.fact: Pairs mate hanging in midair from a tree branch on a thick thread of mucus.

62564.name: Orange-backed Troupial
62564.fact: It tends to skip building a nest and often pirates one from a yellow-rumped cacique instead.

62749.name: Scarce Swallowtail
62749.fact: It's quite common despite the name, which comes from how rarely it reaches Britain.

62796.name: Desert Collared Lizard
62796.fact: Mostly an arthropod eater, it uses strong jaws to take small lizards, snakes and rodents too.

63028.name: Giant Leopard Moth
63028.fact: Mating pairs stay coupled for more than 24 hours, the male walking them between sun and shade while the female folds her legs.

64885.name: Ecuador Poison Frog
64885.fact: Males sing from slightly raised spots to find a female, and the frog's Latin name, bilinguis, comes from its two-pulsed call.

64968.name: American Toad
64968.fact: Fish have reportedly died after eating just one of its toxic tadpoles, but most fish quickly learn to leave them alone.

64970.name: Western Toad
64970.fact: Pick up an adult and it'll often struggle and call out with a sound like a peeping chick.

64972.name: Yosemite Toad
64972.fact: Nicknamed the tiptoeing toad, it has a habit of crossing snowdrifts without letting its belly touch the cold snow.

65564.name: Brown Marsh Frog
65564.fact: It's also called the Baram River frog, after its type locality on the Baram River in Sarawak.

65614.name: Black-striped Frog
65614.fact: Also called the sapgreen stream frog, it lives along gentle streams in evergreen forest, where its tadpoles grow up in the quiet stretches.

65621.name: Bornean Copper-cheeked Frog
65621.fact: Its tadpoles stand out, with dark markings and red gills on a light brown to yellow body, and they're presumably poisonous.

65722.name: Jeju Salamander
65722.fact: Jeju isn't its only home: it also lives on Chindo Island and at the southern tip of the Korean Peninsula.

65982.name: North American Green Frog
65982.fact: Males announce themselves with a call that sounds like a plucked loose banjo string, usually given as a single note.

66007.name: Mink Frog
66007.fact: Named for its scent, said to resemble a mink's, it smells more like rotting onions to anyone who's never sniffed a mink.

66278.name: Strawberry Poison Dart Frog
66278.fact: Mothers carry each tadpole to its own pool of water, often in a bromeliad, then feed it unfertilized eggs that pass on their toxins.

66331.name: Iberian Green Frog
66331.fact: The Sahara frog of North Africa is its closest living relative, and the two may have split when the Mediterranean dried up.

67128.name: South American Common Toad
67128.fact: Once thought to be one species, this toad is really a complex of 16 named species, with others still waiting to be recognized.

67560.name: California Sister
67560.fact: It's called a sister because its black and white forewing markings resemble a nun's habit, and predators find it unpalatable.

67578.name: East Atlantic Sally Lightfoot Crab
67578.fact: Hard to catch by day, it tends to freeze when someone shines a flashlight on it at night, which makes it easy to collect.

68062.name: Gray Wall Jumping Spider
68062.fact: It builds no web, stalking flies on walls instead, and it can take crane flies at least twice its own size.

68137.name: Vervet Monkey
68137.fact: Leopards, martial eagles, rock pythons and baboons each get their own alarm call, which infants learn by observation alone.

68273.name: Pacific Fritillary
68273.fact: Found from California to British Columbia and Alberta, it flies in June and July, and its caterpillars eat Viola ocellata.

68279.name: Rocky Mountain Parnassian
68279.fact: If snow melts before March, its eggs hatch while the stonecrop they eat is still toxic, and the caterpillars die.

68390.name: Giant Golden Orbweaver
68390.fact: Females can be up to ten times the size of males and, unlike other golden orb-weavers, bury their eggs in a pit.

68519.name: Taiga Flycatcher
68519.fact: You can tell it from the red-breasted flycatcher by the female's blackish tail and the breeding male's orange-red, which stops at the throat.

68618.name: China Rockfish
68618.fact: Living up to 79 years, it rarely strays more than 10 meters from its crevice, sometimes shared with a giant Pacific octopus.

69838.name: Lion's Mane Jelly
69838.fact: Detached tentacles can sting for up to 25 days, and in 2010 one broken-up jellyfish is thought to have stung about 150 beachgoers.

69893.name: Inflated Beetle
69893.fact: Its inflated wing covers, black with dense white spots, are fused down the middle, so this beetle can't fly.

70071.name: Leafy Spurge Hawkmoth
70071.fact: Its black caterpillars, dotted white and coral red, eat leafy spurge, so the moth is used to help control that weed.

70128.name: Pine Hawkmoth
70128.fact: Females lay their eggs in twos and threes along pine or spruce needles, which the caterpillars then eat.

70647.name: Eastern Tree Frog
70647.fact: Inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, these tree frogs are much darker on the back, perhaps because the disaster's radiation favored dark skin.

72486.name: Egyptian Goose
72486.fact: A regular in ancient Egyptian art, it's been introduced to Europe and the United States as an ornamental bird.

72504.name: Eastern Spot-billed Duck
72504.fact: Since the early 1900s its range in Japan and the Russian Far East has spread over 500 kilometers north, possibly because of global warming.

72541.name: Puna Thistletail
72541.fact: Males and females both sing a quick run of spluttering high notes that speeds up and grows louder, then fades at the end.

72542.name: Itatiaia Spinetail
