72542.fact: Named for the Serra do Itatiaia, it usually lives above the tree line, from 1,850 to 2,800 meters up.

72936.name: Blue Duck
72936.fact: The male's high-pitched whistle gave it the Māori name whio, and it's pictured on the back of New Zealand's $10 note.

72981.name: Dolphin Gull
72981.fact: It raids seabird nests left empty when people scare the parents off, and keeping humans away has been found to help nesting cormorants.

72994.name: Crested Duck
72994.fact: Along the coast it forages for clams among rocks and kelp, while on the Altiplano it gathers on alkaline lakes thick with zooplankton.

73669.name: Common Spotted Whiptail
73669.fact: Its tail is usually close to three times the length of its body, and males often show a red throat and blue belly.

73691.name: Sonoran Spotted Whiptail
73691.fact: This whiptail is parthenogenic, reproducing without fertilization, and lives in Arizona, New Mexico and Mexico.

73882.name: Indian Roofed Turtle
73882.fact: In October, just before the breeding season, males grow a small knob at the end of their thick tails and shed it in March.

73921.name: Andalusian wall lizard
73921.fact: Swiss botanist Henri Vaucher is honored in its scientific name, and it lives from sea level up to 3,100 meters.

73972.name: Ocellated Lizard
73972.fact: One of the biggest wall lizards, it robs birds' nests for eggs and nestlings and sometimes eats other lizards and small snakes.

74321.name: Thomson's Gazelle
74321.fact: At a shared border, neighboring males hold mock fights, charging without touching, then grazing their way apart with no winner.

74442.name: Capybara
74442.fact: Its meat is popular in Venezuela during Lent, since legend has it the Catholic Church once allowed it while other meats were forbidden.

74532.name: Northern Pig-tailed Macaque
74532.fact: Groups can top 150 monkeys, splitting into smaller parties to feed and coming back together to travel.

74724.name: Grant's Gazelle
74724.fact: Predators are less likely to attack it when it joins a group of Thomson's gazelles, perhaps because the Thomson's make easier targets.

74832.name: Olive Baboon
74832.fact: In Eritrea, olive baboons use water holes dug by elephants, while the elephants use baboons in the treetops as an early warning system.

75256.name: Biddy-biddy
75256.fact: Each fruit carries four barbed spines, red when ripe, that hitch rides on wool, feathers and clothing.

81543.name: Florida Ivory Millipede
81543.fact: Native to Florida and southern Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina, its females grow up to 90 millimeters long.

81645.name: Eastern White Slippersnail
81645.fact: When it lives inside big snail shells taken over by hermit crabs, its own shell often grows extremely flat and curled back.

81677.name: Milkweed Tussock Moth
81677.fact: Adults keep the cardiac glycosides they ate as caterpillars on milkweed and warn bats with ultrasonic clicks that they taste bad.

81731.name: Snowberry Checkerspot
81731.fact: Like the variable checkerspot, its caterpillars feed on plants such as snowberry, then go dormant over winter and pupate in spring.

82003.name: Black Slug
82003.fact: Native to Europe, it's invasive in Australia, Canada, Alaska and the Pacific Northwest, and it eats crops as well as rotting matter.

82069.name: Field Crescent
82069.fact: In Canada it flies from May to August, and its caterpillars feed on plants in the aster family.

82117.name: Dark Fishing Spider
82117.fact: Females eat the males during mating, and research shows that sacrifice improves the odds their young survive.

82201.name: Baltimore Snout
82201.fact: At rest it tucks its hindwings behind its forewings into a triangle, and its caterpillars eat maple, mostly red and silver.

82538.name: New Zealand Red Admiral
82538.fact: Its Māori name, kahukura, means 'red cloak,' and its caterpillars feed on stinging nettles, especially ongaonga.

83089.name: Megalodacne heros
83089.fact: Up to 23 millimeters long, it's the largest pleasing fungus beetle across its range in eastern North America.

83290.name: Moorish Idol
83290.fact: Some Southeast Asian fishermen release it when caught and bow to it afterward, apparently the source of its name.

83297.name: Redlip Parrotfish
83297.fact: It matures as a reddish-brown female and may turn into a greenish-blue male around age 13, though some stay female for life.

83834.name: Isabella's Longwing
83834.fact: Active even in low light, it keeps to the rainforest canopy and flies year-round in the tropics.

83884.name: Lagoon Triggerfish
83884.fact: Mothers guard the eggs for 12 to 14 hours, fanning them with their fins and removing intruding starfish by mouth.

83958.name: California Oak Moth
83958.fact: Its black, yellow-striped caterpillars feed openly by day on oaks, possibly protected by the trees' own defensive chemistry.

84662.name: Northern Azure
84662.fact: On the wing from April to July, it ranges from the Maritimes south along the Appalachians to West Virginia.

93427.name: Azure Hawker
93427.fact: Basking on stones or tree trunks with its wings lowered, it can warm its body as much as 7 degrees Celsius above the air.

94020.name: Bluetail Wrasse
94020.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its other common name, its Pacific range and its maximum length.

94966.name: Jade Hunter
94966.fact: A tiny to medium-sized black and yellow dragonfly, it lives on streams, rivers and lakes from north of Brisbane to Victoria.

94971.name: Dune Ringtail
94971.fact: Its species name, minjerriba, is the Aboriginal name for North Stradbroke Island, where this damselfly of acidic dune lakes was first recorded.

97152.name: Wrought Iron Butterflyfish
97152.fact: Unusually black for a butterflyfish, it sometimes gathers in huge numbers to graze in a tight, rippling 'wrought-iron ball'.

97190.name: Bluespot Butterflyfish
97190.fact: Juveniles have been recorded working as cleaner fish, picking parasites off other fish, while adults feed mostly on coral polyps.

97206.name: Threeband Butterflyfish
97206.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its range, the depths and reefs it lives on and its maximum length.

99684.name: European Edible Sea Urchin
99684.fact: Its name esculentus means edible, but its white gonads, the part that's eaten, make it less prized than urchins with orange ones.

100312.name: Swiss Brassy Ringlet
100312.fact: When the ice retreated about 130,000 years ago, its ancestors followed their habitat uphill and were stranded in different mountain ranges, becoming separate species.

100397.name: Black-winged Dragonlet
100397.fact: Found across North, Central and South America, this skimmer was rated least concern in 2016, with no immediate threat to its survival.

100709.name: Eastern Water Skink
100709.fact: Gaps in its range line up with places where the Great Escarpment is absent, suggesting low ground and dry forest act as barriers.

101053.name: Banded Killifish
101053.fact: Females show thin, crisp black bars while males have fainter, closer-set silvery ones, so the bands tell the sexes apart.

104548.name: Frosted Whiteface
104548.fact: Like every whiteface, it gets the 'whiteface' in its name from the distinctive pale frons at the front of its head.

105329.name: Western Caspian Turtle
105329.fact: It will accept bread from people but lacks the enzymes to digest it, so those handouts are bad for its health.

106415.name: Eastern Saw-shelled Turtle
106415.fact: One of the few native Australian animals that successfully prey on poisonous cane toads, it shreds big ones with its front claws first.

107002.name: Common Parasol
107002.fact: Neurothemis, the first word of its scientific name, pairs the Greek for 'vein' with Themis, the goddess of divine law and order.

107655.name: Boreal Snaketail
107655.fact: Rated secure worldwide, it's critically imperiled in New York, with pollution and dammed waterways among its main threats.

107942.name: White-tailed Skimmer
107942.fact: Patchy but often common from Europe to Japan, it has recently spread north to Poland's Baltic Sea coast.

107955.name: Blue Marsh Hawk
107955.fact: Old males turn powdery blue with a black-tipped abdomen, while females and young males stay golden with brown-striped sides.

107979.name: Little skimmer
107979.fact: Adults hang around open rocky and sandy stream beds in dry zones and hot plains, from eastern Europe to China.

109315.name: European Minnow
109315.fact: An injured minnow releases Schreckstoff, German for 'fear substance', from its skin, and the rest of the shoal bunches tighter together.

109983.name: Chalkhill Blue
109983.fact: It turns in early, settling for the night with its wings closed on grass stalks or flower tops while it's still full daylight.

110927.name: Southern Grass Skink
110927.fact: It gives birth to live young nourished through a complex placenta, and when food runs short females will eat their offspring.

111712.name: Brown Amur Goby
111712.fact: Guarding eggs under a rock for up to two weeks without feeding, a worn-out male may end up eating them.

113517.name: Island Darter
113517.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its family, its range on the Canary Islands and Madeira, its habitat types and a note that it may be a subspecies of the common darter.

114466.name: Crimson Marsh Glider
114466.fact: Males are crimson with a violet tinge and even have crimson wing veins, while females are olive and reddish brown.

114568.name: Bornean Keeled Pit Viper
114568.fact: Females can reach 96 cm, more than twice a male's maximum of 46 cm, and give birth to live young.

114871.name: Canary Red Admiral
114871.fact: Look for it on Madeira and the Canary Islands except Lanzarote, where its caterpillars feed on nettles.

114891.name: Common Water Monitor
114891.fact: Its species name, salvator, means 'savior' in Latin, but in Thailand the lizard's name has long been a swearword.

114956.name: Otway Black Snail
114956.fact: A carnivore, it grips other snails, slugs and earthworms with rows of sharp, backward-pointing teeth, but it won't eat its own kind.

116143.name: Plateau Fence Lizard
116143.fact: A long metallic blue patch runs along each side of its belly, with another on each side of its throat.

116453.name: Many-scaled Anole
116453.fact: Found only around Costa Rica's Golfo Dulce, it bobs its head and flashes an orange-yellow throat fan to attract mates and mark territory.

116461.name: Brown Anole
116461.fact: In the US it has pushed the native green anole up into the treetops, and it sometimes eats green anole hatchlings too.

116523.name: Gharial
116523.fact: The pot-shaped knob on a male's snout, the ghara behind its name, lets him make a hiss that can be heard 75 meters away.

116570.name: Yacare Caiman
116570.fact: Some teeth in its lower jaw poke through holes in its upper jaw, which earned it the name 'piranha caiman'.

116703.name: Ladder Grasshopper
116703.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its other name and that it's a short-horned grasshopper.

116846.name: Glossy Black Cockatoo
116846.fact: Males are blackish brown with bold red tail bands, while females show yellow neck markings and red tail bands barred with black.

116941.name: Common Grasshopper Warbler
116941.fact: It sings its mechanical, grasshopper-like reel with beak wide open and whole body vibrating, often at dawn or dusk.

116999.name: Osprey
116999.fact: On every continent except Antarctica, it hunts almost nothing but fish, though in South America it's only a nonbreeding migrant.

117181.name: Aquatic Warbler
117181.fact: Mainland Europe's rarest passerine, it breeds mostly in the Polesie region of Poland and Belarus, home to 70 percent of the world's population.

117293.name: Asian Weaver Ant
117293.fact: To stitch leaves into a nest, workers wave larvae back and forth across the seams like living shuttles, making them release silk.

117370.name: Small Wood-Nymph
117370.fact: In western North America adults fly from June to August in a single generation, and the caterpillars eat grasses.

117650.name: Blue Mussel
117650.fact: Strong, slightly elastic byssal threads anchor it to rocks, yet it can let go and reattach to shift position.

118474.name: alpine coral-fern
118474.fact: Turn a frond over to find deep, densely hairy pouches under the leaflets, which leave Gleichenia dicarpa as its only lookalike.

118552.name: Domestic Cat
118552.fact: Of an estimated 600 million domestic cats worldwide, 400 million live in Asia, including 58 million in China.

118559.name: Red Milkweed Beetle
118559.fact: When startled it makes a shrill noise, but it purrs when interacting with another beetle.

118832.name: Northern Acorn Barnacle
118832.fact: Its larvae can survive weeks embedded in sea ice and only attach themselves once they've found another barnacle of their own kind.

118851.name: Brown Shrimp
118851.fact: Its numbers at Lytham in Lancashire tracked the yearly sunspot count so closely from 1965 to 1975 that sunspots can help predict the catch.

118970.name: Common Eastern Bumble Bee
118970.fact: Hibernating queens can stay underwater for up to a week without drowning, which may help them survive floods before starting new colonies.

119211.name: Koppie Foam Grasshopper
119211.fact: Its toxic foam comes from glands in the thorax, a mix of haemolymph and air from its spiracles.

119450.name: common heather
119450.fact: Its nectar contains callunene, which makes a common bumble bee parasite lose its flagellum and become less infectious.

121125.name: Centralian Earless Dragon
121125.fact: Tympanocryptis, the first part of its scientific name, means 'hidden ear', and centralis refers to its central Australian range.

121612.name: Salt Marsh Moth
121612.fact: Plant toxins called pyrrolizidine alkaloids don't seem to bother it, and it can detoxify them and even turn them into sex pheromones.

121989.name: Garden Bumble Bee
121989.fact: Its tongue runs about 15 millimeters, so long that it often flies with it sticking out while gathering nectar.

122174.name: Mottled Seahare
122174.fact: A sea hare of the Caribbean and the Atlantic off Brazil, it has a dark brown mantle and a long front end but short rear.

122188.name: Portuguese Millipede
122188.fact: It can survive long sea voyages in a dormant state, and it reached South Australia around 1953, perhaps in ships' ballast.

122515.name: Jack Jumper Ant
122515.fact: Known for jumping long distances, this ant has just one pair of chromosomes.

123346.name: Yellowstripe Goatfish
123346.fact: In Hawaii it's called the 'nightmare weke,' since eating it, especially the head, is said to bring nightmares or hallucinations.

123392.name: Titan Triggerfish
123392.fact: Its nest territory is roughly cone-shaped, so divers should swim away horizontally, because heading up only takes them deeper in.

123455.name: Hayden's Ringlet
123455.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its range and a catalogue number.

123513.name: Tiger Longwing
123513.fact: Like other longwings, its caterpillars eat passion flower vines, and its bright wing pattern warns predators that it tastes bad.

123616.name: faya bayberry
123616.fact: Native to the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores, it's invasive in Hawaii, where it crowds out native trees and deeply alters nitrogen cycling.

123628.name: Silver-washed Fritillary
123628.fact: Unusually for a butterfly, the female lays her eggs in tree bark a meter or two up, close to the violets her caterpillars eat.

123920.name: Lesser Stag Beetle
123920.fact: Adults can't eat solid food, so they get by drinking tree sap and the juice of fallen fruit.

125505.name: Chestnut Tiger
125505.fact: Its pupa is pale emerald green with golden-yellow spots, and eggs laid in September have produced adults the following April.

125555.name: Common Mapwing
125555.fact: Its domed eggs have a toothed lid like a cogwheel, which the caterpillar lifts to climb out, leaving the shell uneaten.

125573.name: Indian Red Admiral
125573.fact: Its caterpillar feeds on nettles and ramie, then folds a leaf, ties the edges together with silk and pupates inside.

125815.name: Pearly Heath
125815.fact: Easy to recognize by the broad white band under its hindwing, it usually sits in sunny spots with its wings closed.

125936.name: Common Bluebottle
125936.fact: Its retinas have 15 types of color-detecting opsins, and its quick flight and rapid reactions make it difficult to catch.

126636.name: Kidney-spot Ladybird
126636.why: No Wikipedia article of its own, and the Chilocorus article is a list of species.

127308.name: Common Field Grasshopper
127308.fact: An interested female answers a male's song with a similar one, and the two can trade songs until they mate or she loses interest.

130079.name: Indian Milkweed Bug
130079.fact: Its Latin name may come from the Panduri, an infantry unit of the Habsburg monarchy, though that was never confirmed.

130166.name: smooth ground beetle
130166.fact: A beetle of the north and of mountains, it's widespread across Central and Northern Europe up to the Arctic Circle.

130213.name: Common Whelk
130213.fact: Look on the beach for its washed-up egg cases, which people call sea wash balls.

130222.name: Black-tailed Bumble Bee
130222.fact: Northern bees wear a red band on the abdomen that's earned them the nickname 'red butts', while southern bees are black there instead.

130451.name: Juno Silverspot
130451.fact: Also called the Juno longwing, it's found from the southern United States all the way down to South America.

130785.name: Northern Blue
130785.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its names and family.

131862.name: Banded Longhorn Beetle
131862.fact: Larvae develop in the decaying wood of trees such as birch and sumac, and it lives in North America.

132319.name: Mottled Grasshopper
132319.fact: Found from the British Isles east to Siberia and south to Morocco, it lives from sea level up to about 2,500 meters.

132892.name: Egyptian Bird Grasshopper
132892.fact: One of Europe's largest grasshoppers, it's easy to identify by its eyes, which have vertical black and white stripes.

134125.name: Swedish Cornel
134125.fact: Its four white 'petals' are really bracts around a tight cluster of small dark purple flowers, and its fruit is a red berry.

143025.name: Bombus balteatus
143025.fact: Its tongue can reach two-thirds of its body length, but in the Rockies it has trended shorter as long-tubed flowers declined.

143291.name: Ash-black Slug
143291.fact: The world's largest land slug can grow past 30 centimeters, but it mostly eats mushrooms and algae and isn't considered a pest.

143853.name: Black-billed Magpie
143853.fact: Once tied to bison herds, it now lands on the backs of cattle to pick off ticks and insects.

144297.name: Great Skua
144297.fact: It often robs gulls, terns and even northern gannets of their fish, and it'll fly at the head of anyone approaching its nest.

144455.name: Great Egret
144455.fact: It nests in tree colonies close to water, and lately it's been spreading into more northern parts of Europe.

144456.name: Pied Heron
144456.fact: Without the adult's crest and dark head, young birds can pass for small white-necked herons and were once classified as a separate species.

144472.name: Black-bellied Bustard
144472.fact: A courting male pulls his head onto his back with a wheezy whistle, then slowly raises it with a popping 'quock' and soft gurgling.

144507.name: Silver Gull
144507.fact: Australia's most common gull, it's known to pester people for chips and to steal food left unattended.

144510.name: Black-headed Gull
144510.fact: Mostly a bird of Europe and Asia, it also breeds in small numbers on the coast of eastern Canada.

144515.name: Franklin's Gull
144515.fact: In spring, big flocks float down rivers like the Bow River sipping hatching insects, then return to float the same stretch again.

144521.name: Pallas's Gull
144521.fact: Easily the world's largest black-headed gull, it's the only gull this big to wear a black hood in summer.

144747.name: Australian Spectacled Monarch
144747.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its range, its forest habitats, its subspecies and the genera it has been moved between.

144757.name: Hooded Crow
144757.fact: A scarce winter visitor to eastern England from Scandinavia, it picked up local names there like 'Royston crow' and 'Danish crow'.

144821.name: Boreal Chickadee
144821.fact: Pairs stay together year round and may mate for life, stashing winter food in caches spread across different trees.

144910.name: Brown-eared Bulbul
144910.fact: One author described its song as 'one of the most unattractive noises made by any bird'.

145081.name: Abyssinian Thrush
145081.fact: Its bill is orange where the African thrush's is yellow, and birds tend to get darker the higher up you go.

145099.name: Indian Pied Starling
145099.fact: The Sema Nagas won't eat this bird because they believe it's the reincarnation of a human.

145153.name: Golden-winged Sunbird
145153.fact: Females that stray into a bronzy sunbird's territory may beg by quivering their wings and fanning their tails, and the bronzy lets them feed.

145157.name: Southern Double-collared Sunbird
145157.fact: The male looks a lot like the greater double-collared sunbird but is smaller, with a narrower red chest band and a shorter bill.

145240.name: Blackpoll Warbler
145240.fact: About the weight of a ballpoint pen, it flies nonstop over open water for an average of 2,500 kilometers each fall.

145245.name: Yellow-rumped Warbler
145245.fact: It's the only warbler that can digest waxy berries like wax myrtle, so its eastern birds sometimes winter as far north as Newfoundland.

145304.name: Pine Siskin
145304.fact: Heavily streaked and drab, though about one bird in a hundred is a green morph that looks more like a Eurasian siskin.

145332.name: Rufous-tailed Weaver
145332.fact: Tanzania is the only country where it breeds, though wandering birds sometimes turn up in Kenya.

145642.name: Pale Grass Blue
145642.fact: After the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, Japanese studies found more abnormalities in pale grass blues exposed to the radiation.

147931.name: Ocola Skipper
147931.fact: Its caterpillars feed on rice and sugarcane, and strays turn up as far north as southern Ontario and New York.

148638.name: Small-eyed Sailor
148638.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its names, who named it, its range and its subspecies, and the Dynamine article is just a list of species.

148672.name: Cross-barred White
148672.fact: Look for it in disturbed spots like forest clearings, roadsides, cattle pastures and wasteland, from the southern United States to Paraguay.

148883.name: Sickle-winged Skipper
148883.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its family and range, and the Eantis genus article is just a list of species.

149448.name: Common Brown
149448.fact: Climate change has it emerging ten days earlier in the year than it did 65 years ago.

153976.name: Black-edged Bark Scorpion
153976.fact: An hour after one researcher was stung, the pain had faded to a tingle like sticking your tongue on a 9-volt battery.

154504.name: Dasymutilla vestita
154504.fact: In one test, only one of five hungry lizards attacked this red-and-black velvet ant, whose bright colors warn predators off.

155403.name: Judolia instabilis
155403.fact: Colors vary from black with yellow spots to all black, and it can be anywhere from 6 to 15 millimeters long.

155504.name: Blue Skimmer
155504.fact: Mature males are powder blue, females are brownish gray, and freshly emerged adults are yellow with black markings.

159228.name: Dwarf Birch
159228.fact: Its bark doesn't peel and is a shiny red-copper, and its small rounded leaves turn red in autumn.

170339.name: European chain fern
170339.fact: It's called chain fern for the linked spore clusters under its fronds, and the frond tips grow new plantlets that take root.

174535.name: Common Streaky-Skipper
174535.fact: Caterpillars feed on mallows, and in Texas several generations of adults fly from March to September.

179994.name: Uinta Ground Squirrel
179994.fact: Only active for a few months each year, adults head back underground to hibernate between late July and mid-August.

179998.name: Columbian Ground Squirrel
179998.fact: Nicknamed 'seven sleepers' for their long hibernation, they greet each other by touching mouths and noses, which looks a lot like kissing.

179999.name: Wyoming Ground Squirrel
179999.fact: Adults head back underground to hibernate by late July, though the year's young stay above ground as late as September.

180001.name: Arctic Ground Squirrel
180001.fact: In hibernation its core body temperature drops below freezing, colder than any other hibernating mammal, and its heart beats about once a minute.

180009.name: Cascade Golden-mantled Ground Squirrel
180009.fact: The Columbia River walls it off from its closest relative, and that isolation likely explains how the two became separate species.

181044.name: Mountain Bumble Bee
181044.fact: It nests underground in abandoned small-mammal burrows, and its colonies are small, often with fewer than 50 workers.

196626.name: Ecuadorian Hermit Crab
196626.fact: After nine hours with one food, it prefers foods that smell different for the next six, like a person bored with the same meal.

197809.name: Cliff Chipmunk
197809.fact: Instead of fattening up like ground squirrels, it keeps food caches that it visits through the cold winter months.

199840.name: House Finch
199840.fact: Sold illegally in New York City as 'Hollywood finches,' birds released in the 1940s went on to settle across the eastern United States.

199875.name: Chocolate-band Snail
199875.fact: It lies dormant through winter in northern Greece but through summer in Crete, with adults digging into the soil and juveniles sheltering under stones.

200008.name: Bogong Moth
200008.fact: Flying by night to the Australian Alps, it may navigate by both the stars and Earth's magnetic field, researchers suggested in 2025.

201031.name: Marabou Stork
201031.fact: Marabous living off garbage dumps will swallow virtually anything, and they've been seen eating shoes and pieces of metal.

201282.name: Eurasian Moorhen
201282.fact: The 'moor' in its name is the old word for marsh, so don't expect to find it out on moorland.

201533.name: Longfin Inshore Squid
201533.fact: Few live a full year, and females lay their jelly egg capsules in communal masses of hundreds on the seafloor.

201995.name: Daemel's Spiny Ant
201995.fact: Like other Polyrhachis ants, it has no stinger and sprays formic acid instead, often while biting, which makes the acid more effective.

202263.name: Asian Magpie Moth
202263.fact: This day-flying moth ranges from India all the way to Samoa, and its caterpillars have been recorded on Brassica plants.

203153.name: Great Tit
203153.fact: Great tits are the first songbirds recorded preying on bats, killing hibernating pipistrelles in winter when other food is scarce and eating their brains.

203759.name: Baltic Macoma
203759.fact: Buried in mud, it feeds through two narrow siphons and can live in water only a tenth as salty as the sea.

204113.name: Red Deer
204113.fact: A rutting stag may guard as many as 20 hinds and rarely eats while he does, losing up to a fifth of his weight.

204114.name: Wapiti
204114.fact: The name wapiti comes from a Shawnee and Cree word for 'white rump', the pale patch it fluffs up to signal alarm.

204472.name: Common Buzzard
204472.fact: Described as 'sluggish and not very bold', a resident buzzard can spend more than half its day just sitting on a perch.

204491.name: Oriental Magpie-Robin
204491.fact: Bangladesh's national bird, known there as the doyel, appears on a banknote and gives its name to Doel Square in Dhaka.

204520.name: New Zealand Pigeon
204520.fact: After eating, it often suns itself, which can ferment the fruit in its crop and leave the bird drunk.

205176.name: Green Grocer
205176.fact: Nymphs spend years underground sipping sap from roots, then adults live about six weeks and males call at up to 120 decibels.

208700.name: American Bison
208700.fact: From 1980 to 1999, bison injured 79 people in Yellowstone, more than three times the 24 hurt by bears.

209233.name: Domestic Horse
209233.fact: Horses usually live 25 to 30 years, but Old Billy, a 19th-century horse, made it to 62, the oldest verifiable record.

209691.name: Lang's Short-tailed Blue
209691.fact: Dark beige underneath with white stripes, it has orange and black spots and two small tails on its hindwings.

209733.name: Sierra Blue
209733.fact: Subalpine meadows in the Klamath Range and Sierra Nevada are its home, and just one generation flies each year, June to September.

210232.name: Peppery Furrow Shell
210232.fact: Star-shaped marks on the surface give away where it's buried, and if fish nibble its siphons, they grow back in a few days.

213110.name: Langton's Forester
213110.fact: Males have eight white spots and females six, and the caterpillars feed on fireweed and related plants.

213611.name: Flamed Tigersnail
213611.fact: Its slime is usually orange or reddish, and these snails often burrow and hibernate together in groups over winter.

213884.name: Apatania zonella
213884.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its family and a one-line range, and the Apatania article is a list of species.

214185.name: Button's Banana Slug
214185.fact: With no shell and a bright, banana-like color, it's protected by toxic slime that numbs the mouth of anything that eats it.

215286.name: Alaskan Fritillary
215286.fact: Also called the mountain fritillary, it's found in North America and northern European Russia, and its caterpillars eat false bistort and alpine smartweed.

219779.name: Anicia Checkerspot
219779.fact: Plant chemicals eaten as a caterpillar stay in its body, and its red, yellow and black bands warn predators that it tastes bad.

219813.name: Eupithecia monticolens
219813.fact: This Hawaiian moth lives on six of the islands and nowhere else, and its caterpillars feed on plants such as Metrosideros and Pipturus.

219829.name: Satyr Pug Moth
219829.fact: Flowers of a wide range of plants feed its caterpillars, and it's found from Ireland to Tibet and in North America too.

221602.name: July Highflyer Moth
221602.fact: The July highflyer lives in the Holarctic, the northern regions of both the Old World and the New World.

225757.name: Uinta Chipmunk
225757.fact: From a rock outcrop or high branch, it can keep up bursts of sharp chip calls for as long as 15 minutes.

228083.name: Banff Springs Snail
228083.fact: Found in a few Banff hot springs and nowhere else, it can dwindle until the entire population fits in an ice cream cone.

228118.name: Arctic White
228118.fact: Males look mostly white from above but can be pale yellow underneath with dark green veins, while females can be white or yellow.

228259.name: Hollow-spotted Plagodis Moth
228259.fact: Summer moths are a paler yellow with fewer markings than the spring brood, and the caterpillars prefer birch.

233598.name: Arctic Fox
233598.fact: A yearling female tagged on Svalbard crossed the polar ice to Greenland and on to Canada, covering 3,506 km in 76 days.

244276.name: New Zealand Fantail
244276.fact: Not shy around people, it often flits within a few meters of them to catch insects stirred up by their walking or digging.

245924.name: Doxocopa linda
245924.fact: Linda's emperor, as it's also called, lives in Peru, Ecuador and the Brazilian state of Amazonas.

254757.name: Well-ribbed Dove Snail
254757.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its family and its range.

257122.name: Faithful Beauty
257122.fact: Nicknamed the Uncle Sam moth, it's a day flier with white-dotted black forewings edged in red and hindwings fading from blue to black.

262223.name: Metaphidippus chera
262223.fact: You can find this jumping spider in both the United States and Mexico.

293720.name: Santa Ana Tussock Moth
293720.fact: Its range runs from southern Texas and Arizona through Mexico and Central America all the way to Argentina.

302724.name: Pictured Rove Beetle
302724.fact: Wingless and nocturnal, it's dark on the volcanic sand north of central California and pale on lighter sand farther south.

307359.name: Western Dobsonfly
307359.fact: Like its close dobsonfly relatives, the male grips the female with huge mandibles when mating, and its larvae, called hellgrammites, hunt underwater.

313246.name: Ashy Gray Lady Beetle
313246.fact: Usually gray or pale tan with small black spots, it also comes in a black form with two red spots on its wing covers.

318758.name: Argentine Black-and-white Tegu
318758.fact: It's one of the few partly warm-blooded lizards, running up to 10 degrees Celsius warmer than its surroundings at night in breeding season.

319989.name: Eastern horse cicada
319989.why: No Wikipedia article of its own, and the Cryptotympana article says only that they're Southeast Asian cicadas.

320711.name: Cory's Shearwater
320711.fact: Silent at sea, it fills its breeding colonies with raucous cackling at night, visiting nests after dark to dodge big gulls.

321995.name: Climbing Galaxias
321995.fact: Broad, downward-facing fins let it climb waterfalls and dam sluices, and young fish netted as whitebait can scramble up and out of buckets.

324831.name: Smoky Wainscot
324831.fact: Hard to tell for certain from similar wainscots, it has buff forewings with a dark streak near the base and gray hindwings edged white.

326296.name: European Toad
326296.fact: Normally solitary, toads gather in large numbers at certain breeding ponds, and some are killed on roads during these annual migrations.

330438.name: Subtropical Lady
330438.fact: Also called the western painted lady, it ranges from the mountains of Colombia down to Patagonia, and is even found on Easter Island.

334019.name: Dewy Ringlet
334019.fact: In the Alps you'll usually meet it only between the tree-line and the snow, and its caterpillar contracts like a slug when touched.

334326.name: Dark Giant Horse Fly
334326.fact: Europe's heaviest fly comes with a very loud buzz, but it usually takes blood only from cows and horses and avoids people.

336013.name: Jewelweed Leaf-miner Fly
336013.fact: Larvae mine the leaves of Himalayan balsam, and adults have a yellow forehead and yellow bands on the thorax.

337496.name: Four-spined Spiny Orbweaver
337496.fact: Unlike most of its spiny relatives, it has just four spines, lacking the usual third pair on the back edge of its abdomen.

338194.name: Asian Honey Bee
338194.fact: In Vietnam, colonies have been found using animal dung and even human urine to defend their hives against hornet raids.

339816.name: Yunnan Fulvetta
339816.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its range, its montane forest habitat and its three subspecies.

339867.name: White-whiskered Laughingthrush
339867.fact: Found only in Taiwan's mountains, it's often seen in large groups and doesn't always shy away from people.

343021.name: Common Slowworm
343021.fact: Possibly the longest-lived lizard, it lives about 30 years in the wild, and one male lived at least 54 years at Copenhagen Zoo.

343588.name: Hidden Hermit Crab
343588.fact: Olive green with dark-tipped legs and a bigger left claw, it often loses out to a close relative when competing for shells.

348016.name: Rufous-legged Grasshopper
348016.fact: Wide black spots mark its slender hind thighs, and young hoppers pass through about five stages before they grow wings.

349178.name: pot-hole urchin
349178.fact: Young ones dig hiding holes in soft rock with their spines, which often leaves the spines strikingly lopsided.

353666.name: Fringed Blue
353666.fact: Like the other two butterflies in its small group, it's found only in Australia and Tasmania.

355743.name: Purple Mussel
355743.why: Its Wikipedia article says only that it's found in South America.

358858.name: Armored Stink Beetle
358858.fact: This desert stink beetle of the dry western United States and Mexico has spurs on all of its legs.

360024.name: Copper Chafer
360024.fact: It lives on pollen until summer, then switches to fruit like apples, and the high-carb fruit lets it travel longer.

361099.name: Texas Glowing Click Beetle
361099.fact: Its light comes from glowing spots on each side of its thorax and a small light organ on its abdomen.

362610.name: Common Halfband
362610.fact: Often confused with Simosyrphus grandicornis, Australia's other most common hoverfly, it's told apart by its all-black thorax.

363775.name: Banded Wedge Shell
363775.fact: Underwater video shows it's most active around low tide, when it 'leaps' and gets dragged around by the waves before burying itself again.

366807.name: gutta bug
366807.why: It has no English Wikipedia article, and the Physopelta article gives only its family, a species count and that they live in Asia and Oceania.

367573.name: White-eyed Parakeet
367573.fact: Its species name, leucophthalmus, means 'white eye' in Greek, but the eye itself is orange, ringed by bare white skin.

367948.name: Arctic Blue
367948.fact: Males are silvery or steely blue above, females almost entirely brown, and the higher up they live, the darker they tend to get.

368940.name: Wide-brand Grass-dart
368940.fact: Its caterpillars feed on Sorghum, Paspalum and Leersia, resting in a shelter made from blades of the plant joined with silk.

370351.name: Little Pied Cormorant
370351.fact: In New Zealand the mostly black, white-throated form wins out, and even in Northland only about one in four birds is pied.

372251.name: Florida Woods Cockroach
372251.fact: When alarmed, adults can shoot a foul-smelling spray up to a meter, which is why it's also called the Florida skunk roach.

387556.name: Australian Pug Moth
387556.fact: Its caterpillars eat flowers, acacia blossoms in Australia and gorse in New Zealand, where it arrived on its own in 1960.

389060.name: Lacebark Looper
389060.fact: Its caterpillar has a white stripe down its back that looks like a leaf vein, camouflaging it on some of its host plants.

394448.name: Creekbed Orange Underwing
394448.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its naming history and that it's endemic to New Zealand.

395366.name: Grey Side-gilled Sea Slug
395366.fact: In 2009 several dogs died after eating these slugs on Auckland beaches, poisoned by tetrodotoxin the slugs likely got from eating dead fish.

397173.name: Sigaus piliferus
397173.fact: Its longer-legged shrubland form and its alpine form, probably separated during the last ice age, now meet among the central North Island volcanoes.

399839.name: Mountain Clubmoss
399839.fact: Upright and conifer-like, this clubmoss grows up to 10 cm tall and can look bright orange in cold conditions.

410365.name: Maui's copper
410365.fact: Found only in New Zealand, its caterpillars feed on Muehlenbeckia, and adults fly from October to April.

410460.name: Common Forest Looper
410460.fact: Endemic to New Zealand, it turned up in a garden light trap in west Cornwall in 2007, the first record outside New Zealand.

411086.name: Western Cattle-Egret
411086.fact: Because it hunts on land, it has lost the ability its wetland relatives have to accurately correct for light refraction by water.

415169.name: Tortoiseshell Limpet
415169.fact: Look for its low, brown-and-white banded shell on stones and boulders crusted with red algae such as Lithothamnion.

418135.name: Stripey
418135.fact: Juveniles are often seen in tide pools, and adults turn up around man-made spots like jetties and harbour walls.

418378.name: Festive Nudibranch
418378.fact: Look for raised pink spots on a white body and a broken yellow line running around the edge of its mantle.

424147.name: European Tree Frog
424147.fact: It croaks as rain approaches, so people once used it as a living barometer.

424747.name: Stripe-tailed Scorpion
424747.fact: Brownish-tan stripes along its tail set it apart from the Arizona bark scorpion, and its venom isn't considered dangerous to people.

425206.name: African Hermit Spider
425206.fact: This African spider has a foothold in Brazil, Colombia and Paraguay too, probably brought over by people in the late 1800s or earlier.

429297.name: Spiny Orb-Weaver Spider
429297.fact: Like other spiny-backed orb-weavers, females are several times larger than the males, which lack the prominent spines and bright colors.

430414.name: Saunder's Case Moth
430414.fact: Also called the large bagworm, it's found across the eastern half of Australia, Tasmania included.

433293.name: frigid bumble bee
433293.fact: Queens leave their winter chambers earlier than other arctic bees and start hunting for a nest site as soon as the snow melts.

433295.name: Lapland Bumble Bee
433295.fact: Many specimens collected as this taiga and tundra bee turn out to be other bumblebees, so its exact range is still unclear.

451072.name: Common piddock
451072.fact: Pliny told of it glowing in the mouths of people who ate it, and it's been known to bore into hard gneiss.

451909.name: Muslin Footman
451909.fact: Its hairy caterpillars eat lichen and mosses, then pupate under rocks and flat stones in a loose cocoon with hairs woven in.

458935.name: Icelandic Scallop
458935.fact: Subfossil shells of this North Atlantic scallop turn up south of its present range, including in the British Isles.

461788.name: Rhagonycha nigritarsis
461788.why: It has no Wikipedia article, and the Rhagonycha genus article gives only its family, range, species count and fossil age.

464739.name: Isogona snowi
464739.fact: Snow's owlet flies year round in southern Texas and Mexico, and its caterpillars feed on Celtis pallida.

465333.name: Mytilene Bright Bush-Cricket
465333.fact: Bright bush crickets are named for their often bright colors, and their antennae run about three times the length of their body.

465767.name: Common Digging Grasshopper
465767.fact: A band-winged grasshopper, it turns up across three continents: Europe, Africa and Asia.

467422.name: Lophyra flexuosa
467422.fact: Called the leopard tiger beetle, it can fly and ranges from France and Spain across North Africa to Israel and Syria.

467427.name: Scarabaeus cicatricosus
467427.fact: Like its relative the sacred scarab, it feeds only on dung, rolling a piece away from the pile and burying it to eat underground.

468017.name: Brown-hooded Cockroach
468017.fact: Its young hatch eyeless and without the gut microbes that digest wood, so the parents pass those on by feeding them hindgut fluid.

469590.name: Black-spotted Falsehorn
469590.fact: Adults are strong wasp mimics, while the larvae burrow through moist, decayed wood.

469884.name: Cytheris Fritillary
469884.fact: Underneath, its hindwings are dark red with a narrow white streak near the middle, while the forewings are sandy orange.

471139.name: Copris ochus
471139.why: It has no English Wikipedia article, and the Copris article only says the genus has more than 250 tunnelling species found almost worldwide.

472766.name: Eurasian Kestrel
472766.fact: An old name for it is windhover, from its habit of hovering in the air, and kestrels were once used to keep pigeons away.

473586.name: Traulia ornata
473586.fact: A short-horned grasshopper with an Asian range, it's found in the south and east of the continent.

473975.name: Silver Princess
473975.why: Its Wikipedia article says only that it's a cicada found in southeastern Australia, and the Yoyetta article gives just the genus's naming history and range.

475125.name: Wedge-tailed Shearwater
475125.fact: Pairs bond for several years, though a breeding season that ends in failure can lead to divorce.

483726.name: Cranberry Blue
483726.fact: True to its name, its caterpillars feed on cranberry and bilberry, and it flies low on very broad, rounded wings.

484297.name: Leptura annularis
484297.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its family and who described it.

485402.name: Naked Green Sea Urchin
485402.why: Its Wikipedia article says only that it's a spiny sea urchin and who described it, and the Arbacia article is a list of species.

485806.name: Striped Venus
485806.fact: The surest way to tell it from the common venus clam is its siphons, fully joined here but separate and much shorter in the other.

486630.name: Eastern Buzzard
486630.why: Its Wikipedia article covers only its split from the common buzzard and where its four subspecies live.

487192.name: Pretty Orbweaver
487192.fact: Its diamond-shaped abdomen ranges from reddish-brown to bright green or yellow on top, with a jet-black block edged in white or yellow below.

490837.name: Middle Eastern Flower Scarab
490837.fact: These day-active chafers often feed on flowers, and each species has its own distinctive pattern, usually white dots or lines on black.

491075.name: Pimelia muricata
491075.fact: Fused body plates help it hold on to water, but they also leave it unable to fly.

492519.name: North Island Robin
492519.fact: Mates raid each other's food caches, and a robin is less likely to stash food while its partner is around.

499399.name: Short-winged Rice Grasshopper
499399.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its subfamily, its range and where the type specimen was collected.

500625.name: Amarygmus morio
500625.fact: Its wireworm-shaped larvae are shiny and mostly yellow-brown, and some have been collected from the trunk of a rotting mango tree.

503374.name: Eastern Black-tailed Rattlesnake
503374.fact: True to its name, its tail scales are entirely black, no matter what color the rest of the snake is.

506118.name: California Scrub-Jay
506118.fact: It summons other jays to screech over a dead jay, and these noisy 'funerals' can last up to half an hour.

508982.name: Yellow-throated Honeyeater
508982.fact: Endemic to Tasmania, it collects hair for its nest straight from live animals, including horses, dogs and people.

510166.name: Blueberry Hermit Crab
510166.fact: Blue to purple with pale eyestalks, it chirps at a high pitch by rapidly beating the tip of its body inside its shell.

510205.name: Marbled Ringlet
510205.fact: Its name comes from the underside of its hindwings, marbled in chestnut brown with clearly marked whitish veins.

512161.name: Bradfield's Hornbill
512161.fact: An uncommon bird of mopane woodland, it has white tips on its long tail and a long bill with no casque.

512251.name: ʻIʻiwi
512251.fact: Its song has been likened to whistles, balls dropping into water, balloons rubbing together and the squeak of a rusty hinge.

516126.name: Culpeo
516126.fact: The Selk'nam people of Tierra del Fuego domesticated it, producing the Fuegian dog, which died out around the turn of the 20th century.

517053.name: Guttural Toad
517053.fact: After about 75 days as tadpoles, young toads can leave the ponds in such numbers that they carpet the ground.

517119.name: Giant Toad
517119.fact: Rhinella, the first word of its scientific name, means 'little nose', built from the Greek for nose and a Latin ending for small.

518869.name: Spiny-legged Stingless bee
518869.fact: Unable to sting, it defends the nest by tangling itself in a person's hair, buzzing loudly and crawling into their ears and nose.

540190.name: Island Fence Lizard
540190.fact: On California's Channel Islands, the only place it lives, males do head-bobs and pushups to show off blue throats and bellies.

543672.name: Bark-mimicking Grasshopper
543672.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its name and that it lives in Australia.

547200.name: Chestnut-cheeked Starling
547200.fact: It breeds in Japan, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, then heads south to spend winter in Taiwan, the Philippines and northern Borneo.

556687.name: Chameleon Grasshopper
556687.fact: Most grasshoppers stay passive or chirp to settle disputes, but this one is known among entomologists for frequent, escalated physical fights.

567360.name: Yellow-banded Pinktoe Tarantula
567360.fact: Often mistaken for Avicularia juruensis, it has brighter yellow leg rings, and an antifungal peptide in its venom was named juruin after the mix-up.

568268.name: Phimenes curvatus
568268.fact: A potter wasp, it belongs to a group found across the Indomalayan and Australasian regions.

597463.name: Tropical Boubou
597463.fact: Its bou, hou and boubou calls give it its name, and pairs duet so fast they sound like one bird.

605066.name: Cape Protea Chafer
605066.fact: Also called the brunia beetle, this flower scarab is found only in South Africa's Cape Floristic Region.

618828.name: Solor Jawfish
618828.why: It has no Wikipedia article, and the Opistognathus article gives only the oceans the jawfish live in and a list of species.

619598.name: Japanese Angelfish
619598.fact: Females turn into males when they reach 12.7 cm long, and the switch takes 20 to 39 days to finish.

681171.name: Rough Thicktail Scorpion
681171.fact: Like nearly all thick-tailed scorpions, it makes a warning sound by rubbing its sting against the rough base of its tail.

694796.name: Mayan Moth
694796.fact: This moth's known range is southern Africa, where it's been found in South Africa and Zimbabwe.

700910.name: Diervilla Clearwing
700910.fact: Its caterpillars' only known host plant is northern bush honeysuckle, so this bumblebee mimic's range is limited by where the honeysuckle grows.

740644.name: Ezo Spring Cicada
740644.why: There's no English Wikipedia article for it or its genus, Yezoterpnosia.

742930.name: Bay Nettle
742930.fact: It eats the comb jellies that hurt Chesapeake Bay fisheries, and their impact fades once bay nettles reach high numbers each summer.

748473.name: Coriomeris hirticornis
748473.why: It has no English Wikipedia article, and the genus article gives only its family and a species count.

750900.name: greater-streaked shieldbug
750900.why: It has no English Wikipedia article, and the genus article only lists its species.

782146.name: Nyctelia confusa
782146.why: No Wikipedia article for it or for Nyctelia, and the Nycteliini article says only that the tribe has about 12 genera in the Neotropics.

790501.name: Eleodes pilosa
790501.fact: Like other pinacate beetles, it's flightless and defends itself with quinone-type chemicals, which many of its relatives spray while standing on their heads.

791928.name: scarlet pimpernel
791928.fact: Its flowers open only in sunshine and close when it clouds over, which earned it names like shepherd's weather glass.

792926.name: Bearded Woodpecker
792926.fact: One of Africa's largest woodpeckers, it drums loudly on branches and ends each drum-roll with four taps.

793157.name: Black-crested Bulbul
793157.fact: Look for a black crested head with a yellow eye, and in central and eastern Thailand, a red throat as well.

797594.name: Uganda blue-headed tree agama
797594.why: Its Wikipedia article says only that it's a small lizard found in Uganda and Tanzania, and the Acanthocercus genus article gives just a range.

797597.name: Peters's Rock Agama
797597.fact: By eating Florida's invasive brown anoles, it may leave mosquitoes fewer to feed on and send them after people, a 2024 study suggests.

797638.name: Taiwan Japalure
797638.fact: A sit-and-wait hunter that eats mostly ants, it's native to Taiwan but has turned up as an invasive species in Japan.

814777.name: Paragymnopleurus ambiguus
814777.fact: Like its close relatives, this Asian dung beetle has a broad, shovel-shaped head and strong legs with large teeth along the outside.

825289.name: African Wolf
825289.fact: Long mistaken for a golden jackal, it was shown by DNA studies in 2015 to be closer to gray wolves and coyotes.

827401.name: Oriental Magpie
827401.fact: Korean children were taught to toss a lost tooth onto the roof while singing to the magpie, which would bring a new one.

827413.name: Morelet's Seedeater
827413.fact: Meant to honor the collector Morelet, its scientific name came out misspelled as morelleti, and naming rules say the typo stays.

874749.name: Yellow-legged Pachyiulus
874749.why: No Wikipedia article, and the Pachyiulus article is a list of species.

893613.name: Pome Looper
893613.why: Its Wikipedia article gives only its family, who named it, its island range and a note that adults come to light.

904339.name: Redleg Orbweaver
904339.fact: Strong enough to snag the occasional bird or bat, its web is spun from yellow silk that shines like gold in sunlight.

904341.name: Tiger Spider
904341.fact: This orb weaver packs uneaten prey into a storage band near its web's hub and eats from it when catches are poor.

922180.name: Vineyard Snail
922180.fact: Its scientific name comes from Vindobona, the Celtic settlement now known as Vienna, the capital of Austria.

937415.name: Eastern Short-eared Rock Wallaby
937415.fact: Once lumped in with the Kimberley's short-eared rock-wallaby, it's smaller and darker, with brighter limbs and bolder stripes on its head and flanks.

963673.name: Camponotus hemichlaena
963673.fact: Carpenter ants like this one don't eat wood, and despite the name, only a few kinds even nest in it.

966787.name: grass snake
966787.fact: It can rear up and flatten its head and neck like a cobra, a trick that may date from when cobras lived in Europe.

974703.name: Alpine Treasure Owlet
974703.fact: Nobody has confirmed what its caterpillars eat in the wild, and ones raised from eggs in captivity didn't make it to adulthood.

980095.name: Rainbow Lorikeet
980095.fact: According to BirdLife Australia's annual census, it's the most commonly observed bird in Australia.

980262.name: Warbling White-eye
980262.fact: In Japan it's called mejiro, meaning "white eye," and it shows up often in Japanese art and was once kept as a cage bird.

1021509.name: Gray Buckeye
1021509.fact: Its wing eyespots distract predators just like the common buckeye's, and until 2018 it was counted as part of that species.

1081329.name: Zabulon Skipper
1081329.fact: Males are mostly orange and perch all day looking for females, which are dark brown with large glassy spots.

1090483.name: Carabus gehinii
1090483.fact: Hunting snails at night, Carabus beetles like this one either crush the shell or push their heads inside to eat.

1095846.name: White beggarticks
1095846.fact: Each plant yields around 1,200 seeds, and it can regrow from its stems, which is why it spreads so fast as a weed.

1127596.name: Salish Sea Sandpirate
1127596.why: It has no Wikipedia article of its own, and its genus article, Lasiopogon (fly), is only a list of species.

1127950.name: Inland Hooded Snake
1127950.fact: A solid glossy black hood covers the top of its head and nape, set against a brick-red back and white belly.

1144216.name: Long-nosed Swamp Fly
1144216.fact: Adults show a striped thorax and sawtooth yellow spots on the abdomen, and the larvae live in water.

1154098.name: Brown Longtail
1154098.fact: Its caterpillars feed on grasses, including Bermuda grass and Johnson grass, and southern Texas sees three generations a year.

1210965.name: Side-striped Jackal
1210965.fact: Less of a hunter than other jackals, one was recorded slipping into a duck pen to eat the ducks' feed and ignoring the birds.

1223390.name: East Aegean Green Lizard
1223390.why: Its Wikipedia article is a two-line stub that gives only its family and range.

1225676.name: Wahlberg’s Striped Skink
1225676.fact: The Wahlberg in its name was Johan August Wahlberg, a Swedish naturalist, and this skink gives birth to live young.

1242736.name: Purple Olive Snail
1242736.fact: Native Californians have made beads from its shell for at least 9,000 years, and such beads have been found as far inland as Idaho.

1289591.name: Imperial Shag
1289591.fact: It nests in colonies often shared with rockhopper penguins and black-browed albatrosses, cementing seaweed and grass together with mud and droppings.

1289600.name: Magellanic Cormorant
1289600.fact: Feeding close to shore along kelp beds, it typically dives only about 5 meters, leaving deeper water further out to the imperial shag.

1289601.name: Neotropic Cormorant
1289601.fact: Groups sometimes beat the water with their wings to drive fish into the shallows, and unlike other cormorants it often perches on wires.

1321829.name: Marbled Skipper
1321829.fact: Its darker hindwings carry two rows of almost white spots, and it has just one generation a year, flying from May to July.

1367786.name: orange pore fungus
1367786.fact: Nicknamed the orange Ping-Pong bat for its shape, it's been in New Zealand since the 1950s but wasn't collected in mainland Australia until 2004.

1369296.name: Central American White-faced Capuchin
1369296.fact: On Jicarón Island, male capuchins took up a fad of kidnapping baby howler monkeys and carrying them around on their backs.

1422071.name: three spot skipper
1422071.fact: The caterpillars eat four kinds of Lepidosperma as well as Phlebocarya ciliata, and adults have a wingspan of about 35 millimeters.

1424115.name: Southern Crested Guineafowl
1424115.fact: A courting male may run several meters to the hen to present her with a particular morsel.

1424710.name: Roughtail Rock Agama
1424710.fact: Its dung was once imported from the Levant to European pharmacies and used as an eye medicine and a cosmetic.

1425711.name: Malayan Crested Fireback
1425711.fact: Look for white central tail feathers and red legs, which set it apart from the Bornean crested fireback it was once lumped with.

1430934.name: Damara Dik-dik
1430934.fact: Dik-diks are named for their call, a trumpet-like 'zik-zik' they give while zigzagging away from danger to a nearby thicket.

1432781.name: Chimango Caracara
1432781.fact: The commonest raptor through much of Chile and Argentina, it often follows farmers as they plow, sometimes more than 100 birds at once.

1439800.name: Pacific Creolefish
1439800.fact: Unlike most groupers, it schools in the water column and picks plankton one at a time, but it still hides in crevices from danger.

1441747.name: Dusky Eagle-Owl
1441747.fact: One of the world's least studied owls, it reuses stick nests of other large birds, in Haryana mostly those of woolly-necked storks.

1453431.name: Red-necked Wallaby
1453431.fact: Courtship starts with the female licking the male's neck, and the pair even spar briefly, standing upright like two males, before mating.

1453434.name: Tammar Wallaby
1453434.fact: It can survive by drinking seawater, which lets it live on several islands that have no fresh water.

1454382.name: Double-crested Cormorant
1454382.fact: The auritum in its scientific name comes from the Latin for 'eared', after the same breeding crests above its eyes that make it double-crested.

1455918.name: Spotted Dove
1455918.fact: Watch for the white-spotted black collar on the back and sides of its neck, and the explosive flutter when it takes off from the ground.

1455922.name: Laughing Dove
1455922.fact: Western Australia's population started with birds released from Perth Zoo in 1898, which then established themselves in the wild.

1456607.name: Dark Green Fritillary
1456607.fact: Across the Palearctic, it ranges from Europe and Morocco through Iran, Siberia and Central Asia to China, Korea and Japan.

1473498.name: Podarcis lusitanicus
1473498.fact: Look for this lizard in Portugal and Spain, the two countries where it's found.

1475913.name: Great Mormon
1475913.fact: Females come in many forms, a lot of them mimics of unpalatable butterflies, and it's been studied extensively for the genetics of that mimicry.

1505007.name: Ornate Sunbird
1505007.fact: Using grass, moss, lichens and spider webs, the female builds a hanging nest up to 60 cm long with a hooded side entrance.

1505779.name: Plumed Egret
1505779.fact: In breeding season it grows long, frilly white plumes on its breast and shoulders, and its bill turns red or orange.

1507371.name: Wurflen's Bumble Bee
1507371.fact: This is a widespread bumblebee of Europe, found in the continent's mountainous regions.

1510571.name: Southern Giraffe
1510571.fact: Also called the two-horned giraffe, it has rounded or blotched spots, some with star-like points, running all the way down to its hooves.

1510574.name: Maasai Giraffe
1510574.fact: Tanzania's national animal, it has jagged, leaf-like blotches that run all the way from its hooves to its head.

1551487.name: Flying Crab
1551487.fact: It feeds on crustaceans, especially young Crangon shrimp, as well as molluscs and fish, and can host the parasitic barnacle Sacculina.

1578489.name: American Herring Gull
1578489.fact: To crack clams and mussels, it drops them from a height onto roads or rocks, a habit that seems to be learned.

1585912.name: Cape Robin-Chat
1585912.fact: Its harsh, three-syllable alarm call is behind local names like 'Jan frederik', which fits the rhythm if you run the last syllables together.

1592009.name: Lanna Green Pitviper
1592009.fact: Like every Asian palm pit viper, it has venom that mainly attacks the blood and is considered medically significant to humans.

1607274.name: Casbia tetramera
1607274.why: No Wikipedia article, and the Casbia article is a list of species.

1630133.name: Rainbow Skink
1630133.fact: Three yellow-orange stripes run from its head to an electric blue tail, though in adults they can fade until they're hard to see.

1638386.name: Northern Cloudywing
1638386.fact: Both sexes have dark brown wings all over except for small, clear triangular spots, and caterpillars pupate rolled up in a leaf.

1641936.name: Ecuadorian Squirrel Monkey
1641936.fact: At 34 to 44 cm, its tail is longer than its head and body put together.

1651488.name: White-headed Woodpecker
1651488.fact: Birds on southern California's mountaintops have longer bills, apparently an adaptation for feeding on the large, spiny cones of Coulter pines.

1668965.name: Japanese Tree Frog
1668965.fact: Males space out their calls so females can locate each one, a trick people have copied to design wireless networks with no central hub.

1673443.name: Desert Spiny Lizard
1673443.fact: A frequent tree climber, it favors cottonwoods, yuccas, Joshua trees and ironwood, and is often seen doing territorial push-ups.

1696537.name: Wisent
1696537.fact: When poachers killed the last free-living wisent in 1927, Europe's heaviest wild land animal was down to 48, all in zoos.
